items.content: Back to Articles Multimodal open d1 decision models for the edge Team Article Published October 7, 2026 Upvote 27 +21 Aurelien Lac Aurelien-Lac Follow LiquidAI Fernando Fernandes Neto fernandofernandes Follow LiquidAI Edoardo Mosca EdoardoMosca Follow LiquidAI Maxime Labonne mlabonne Follow LiquidAI Leonie Monigatti iamleonie Follow LiquidAI Today, we release two open decision models in our d1 decision model family : d1-3B and d1-omni-600M (experimental). Best decision model under 10B on the Decision Index 0.2.1: d1-3B scores 48.57, ahead of every 4B and 9B model and of Decider 35B-A3B (47.11). Multimodal: d1-3B supports text and images, while d1-omni-600M supports text and images or text and audio Fast: d1-3B answers a question in 16 ms on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor, 26 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin, and 50ms on a Jetson Orin Nano How we built decision models for the edge These open d1 decision models are built on our Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs). Unlike our generative models, decision models don’t produce tokens but answer in a single forward pass. d1-3B and d1-omni-600M are trained from two very different backbones: d1-3B is trained from LFM2.5-VL-3B , our latest VLM, which is decoder-only. It accepts text and images as inputs. d1-omni-600M is trained from LFM2.5-Encoder-350M , a bidirectional encoder. It adds vision and audio encoders to handle all three modalities. It accepts either text and image, or text and audio as inputs. This model is currently in an early research release and is undergoing further development. Benchmark results We benchmarked d1-3B and d1-omni-600M on seven public datasets spanning reading comprehension, toxicity detection, intent classification, medical QA, and cross-lingual understanding. d1-3B achieves a mean score of 82.9, the highest in the table and above Decider 4B. d1-omni-600M scores 78.4, surpassing Decider 2B (77.1) with only a quarter of the parameters. Benchmark d1-omni-600M d1-3B Decider 2B Decider 4B SQuAD 2.0 74.0 83.3 67.7 76.0 Civil Comments 95.8 93.3 93.6 92.8 MASSIVE intent 86.1 86.9 81.1 88.3 PubMedQA 61.3 68.3 65.7 63.3 BoolQ 77.7 86.3 87.3 89.0 XNLI 74.7 85.6 85.0 88.6 PAWS-X 79.5 76.4 59.5 69.8 Mean 78.4 82.9 77.1 81.1 We validated that d1-3B retains the vision capabilities of its LFM2.5-VL-3B backbone on standard vision benchmarks, and that d1-omni-600M handles all three modalities. We do not report any vision or audio benchmarks, as the Decision Index v0.3 includes only a private vision split and audio decision benchmarks are currently an open problem. Speed In collaboration with NVIDIA, we evaluated d1-3B on the NVIDIA stack across NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090, NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor, Jetson AGX Orin 64 GB, and Jetson Orin Nano. Since d1-omni-600M is an early research release, we don’t report any speed numbers for it in this release. Edge inference. d1-3B answers a single question in under 50 ms on every measured device. Three questions take only 1.3x the time of one, with the AGX Thor going from 16 ms to 20 ms. One question 3 questions 3.4K-token state 384px image 64 states, packed Apple M5 Pro 30 ms 41 ms 640 ms 62 ms 78 / s Jetson AGX Thor 16 ms 20 ms 220 ms 35 ms 262 / s Jetson AGX Orin 64 GB 26 ms 35 ms 560 ms 83 ms 110 / s Jetson Orin Nano 50 ms 73 ms 1,640 ms 202 ms 38 / s GPU inference. On GPU, d1-3B answers a question in under 10 ms and processes a 384px image in under 18 ms on both platforms. One question 3 questions 3.4K-token state 384px image 64 states, packed NVIDIA RTX 4090 8 ms 21 ms 102 ms 17 ms 475 / s AMD MI325X 9 ms 14 ms 44 ms 18 ms 1,106 / s How to use open d1 decision models Reach for d1 decision models when you need fast, structured decisions, including multimodal inputs. d1-3B delivers the highest decision quality at its size, while d1-omni-600M fits where footprint matters. Install the dependencies (requires transformers>=5.14 ): pip install "transformers>=5.14" torch torchvision pillow These model ship their own code, so load it with trust_remote_code=True : import io import urllib.request import torch from PIL import Image from transformers import AutoModel device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "mps" if torch.backends.mps.is_available() else "cpu" model = AutoModel.from_pretrained( "LiquidAI/d1-3B" , trust_remote_code= True , dtype=torch.float32 if device == "cpu" else torch.bfloat16).to(device) # Several named questions over one text state, answered in one pass questions = { "refund" : { "type" : "noul" , "instructions" : "Is the customer asking for a refund?" }, "team" : { "type" : "choice" , "instructions" : "Which team should handle this?" , "criteria" : { "billing" : "Charges, refunds, invoices" , "technical" : "App or site faults" , "fraud" : "Suspected unauthorised use" }}, "urgency" : { "type" : "score" , "instructions" : "How urgent is this?" , "criteria" : [ "Can wait" , "Today" , "Blocking the customer now" ]}, } print (model.system_one( "I was charged twice this month, please refund one of them." , questions)) # An image as the whole state url = "http://images.cocodataset.org/val2017/000000039769.jpg" # two cats on a sofa photo = Image. open (io.BytesIO(urllib.request.urlopen(url).read())) print (model.system_one( None , { "cats" : { "type" : "choice" , "instructions" : "How many cats are there?" , "criteria" : { "one" : "One" , "two" : "Two" , "more" : "Three or more" }}}, images=[photo])) # Many requests, packed together with no padding tickets = [ "Where is my parcel? It was due Monday." , "The app crashes when I open settings." ] print (model.system_one_batch([(t, { "team" : questions[ "team" ]}) for t in tickets])) For brevity, we only include the example for d1-3B. See the d1-omni-600M model card for instructions on how to run it. Get Started with open d1 decision models Both decision models are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today: Download: d1-3B and d1-omni-600M on Hugging Face. Try: run the demos in our System One Arcade Hugging Face Space. We can't wait to see what you build. items.content: Back to Articles The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself Published October 8, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 5 yuvraj sharma ysharma Follow Abubakar Abid abidlabs Follow Last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern , and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16. Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern plans the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware. How I prompt ML Intern The first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts , exactly as I wrote them. A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally says "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub issues made the fallback trainer risky. Two lines in the prompt are critical . The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt says: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run. At the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer. You don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days. 1. A model that knows your field A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand. On the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90. Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App 2. A model that draws your character Image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B , trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset. The agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model . From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60. Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App 3. A model that does a new trick Camera-angle LoRAs are among the most-liked community add-ons for earlier Qwen-Image models. You can give the model a picture of an object and ask to see it 45 degrees from the left. When I checked a few days after the Qwen-Image 2.1 model release, nobody had made one, so I tasked ML-intern to build it. ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions. Training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16. Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App Doodle-in LoRA is another cool idea. Upload a photo with a magenta scribble on it and add a short prompt naming an object. The LoRA replaces the scribble with that object while keeping the original lighting and composition consistent. No dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely. Before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500. Paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24. Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App 4. A model that fits your device The Pocket Rewriter from the top of this post is the first one. ML-intern started by generating 8,797 short image requests with a small instruct model through Inference Providers, following a mix set in my prompt: photos, posters, logos, infographics and more, about a third of them asking for exact text in quotes, and many in languages other than English. The 9B teacher then rewrote all of them on one A100 in 2 hours 37 minutes (~USD 6.50). After filtering for quality, 1,840 examples were selected for training dataset. Training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16. Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena Agate-Preview-002-4step is the second. Logolabs' Agate Preview 002 is a 260M-parameter text-to-image model, small enough for a browser, but it needs 50 steps with guidance, which is 100 network passes per image. I asked ML-intern to distill it down to just 4 passes! It took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22. I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37. Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE What it cost Model Base model Compute Citrus Doctor Qwen3.5-2B USD 1.90 Huggy LoRA FLUX.2 klein base 4B USD 7.60 Pocket rewriter (0.8B and 2B) Qwen3.5-0.8B and 2B USD 16.05 Viewpoint Orbit LoRA Qwen-Image 2.1 USD 16 Doodle-in LoRA Qwen-Image 2.1 USD 24.30 Agate 4-step (two runs) Agate Preview 002 USD 37 Total about USD 103 These are the GPU and CPU job charges reported for each session. Make yours ML-intern is in HuggingChat . Switch on ML-intern mode and paste a prompt. If you want a starting point, my example prompts are free to copy. Start from a model you wish existed and a dataset you have, or one you can describe. Give it a small budget, ask for a baseline and a smoke test, and read what comes back before you raise the cap. If you make something with it, share it on X and tag @Gradio and @HuggingFace . We would love to see the models you make that nobody else would think to build for you. ML-intern plans the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware. How I prompt ML Intern The first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts , exactly as I wrote them. A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally says "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub issues made the fallback trainer risky. Two lines in the prompt are critical . The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt says: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run. At the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer. You don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days. 1. A model that knows your field A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand. On the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90. Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App 2. A model that draws your character Image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B , trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset. The agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model . From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60. Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App 3. A model that does a new trick Camera-angle LoRAs are among the most-liked community add-ons for earlier Qwen-Image models. You can give the model a picture of an object and ask to see it 45 degrees from the left. When I checked a few days after the Qwen-Image 2.1 model release, nobody had made one, so I tasked ML-intern to build it. ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions. Training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16. Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App Doodle-in LoRA is another cool idea. Upload a photo with a magenta scribble on it and add a short prompt naming an object. The LoRA replaces the scribble with that object while keeping the original lighting and composition consistent. No dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely. Before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500. Paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24. Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App 4. A model that fits your device The Pocket Rewriter from the top of this post is the first one. ML-intern started by generating 8,797 short image requests with a small instruct model through Inference Providers, following a mix set in my prompt: photos, posters, logos, infographics and more, about a third of them asking for exact text in quotes, and many in languages other than English. The 9B teacher then rewrote all of them on one A100 in 2 hours 37 minutes (~USD 6.50). After filtering for quality, 1,840 examples were selected for training dataset. Training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16. Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena Agate-Preview-002-4step is the second. Logolabs' Agate Preview 002 is a 260M-parameter text-to-image model, small enough for a browser, but it needs 50 steps with guidance, which is 100 network passes per image. I asked ML-intern to distill it down to just 4 passes! It took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22. I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37. Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE What it cost Model Base model Compute Citrus Doctor Qwen3.5-2B USD 1.90 Huggy LoRA FLUX.2 klein base 4B USD 7.60 Pocket rewriter (0.8B and 2B) Qwen3.5-0.8B and 2B USD 16.05 Viewpoint Orbit LoRA Qwen-Image 2.1 USD 16 Doodle-in LoRA Qwen-Image 2.1 USD 24.30 Agate 4-step (two runs) Agate Preview 002 USD 37 Total about USD 103 These are the GPU and CPU job charges reported for each session. Make yours ML-intern is in HuggingChat . Switch on ML-intern mode and paste a prompt. If you want a starting point, my example prompts are free to copy. Start from a model you wish existed and a dataset you have, or one you can describe. Give it a small budget, ask for a baseline and a smoke test, and read what comes back before you raise the cap. If you make something with it, share it on X and tag @Gradio and @HuggingFace . We would love to see the models you make that nobody else would think to build for you. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.12449 (cs) [Submitted on 8 Oct 2026] Title: Bi-FORK: Generative Modeling of High-Dimensional Bifurcating Systems Authors: Anna Zimmel , Fleur Hendriks , Markus Holzleitner , Florian Sestak , Martin Weichselbaumer , Vlado Menkovski , Johannes Brandstetter View a PDF of the paper titled Bi-FORK: Generative Modeling of High-Dimensional Bifurcating Systems, by Anna Zimmel and 6 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Bifurcations are ubiquitous in physical systems, from structural buckling to fluid and climate dynamics, yet they remain largely unexplored in deep learning. At a symmetry-breaking bifurcation, a single input admits multiple equally valid solutions, violating the one-to-one assumption underlying most learned physical surrogates. We introduce Bi-FORK, a generative framework for learning these one-to-many solution maps in high-dimensional systems. Bi-FORK generates complete trajectories through latent flow matching, preserving space and time coherence, and uses repulsion-guided sampling to recover distinct solution branches in a single amortized pass. We evaluate Bi-FORK on buckling beams, mechanical metamaterials, and Allen-Cahn phase separation, spanning continuous, discrete, and field-valued bifurcations with discretizations up to 260,000 points. Bi-FORK recovers the multimodal solution structure while scaling several orders of magnitude beyond prior approaches, opening generative modeling to high-dimensional bifurcating physical systems. items.content: Bi-FORK: Generative Modeling of High-Dimensional Bifurcating Systems Anna Zimmel Fleur Hendriks Markus Holzleitner Florian Sestak Affiliation: ELLIS Unit, LIT AI Lab, Institute for Machine Learning, JKU Linz Affiliation: Department of Mathematics and Computer Science, Eindhoven University of Technology Email: zimmel@ml.jku.at Martin Weichselbaumer Vlado Menkovski Johannes Brandstetter * Equal contribution as first authors, † Equal contribution as last authors Affiliation: ELLIS Unit, LIT AI Lab, Institute for Machine Learning, JKU Linz Affiliation: Department of Mathematics and Computer Science, Eindhoven University of Technology Affiliation: Mistral, Paris Email: f.hendriks@differ.nl Affiliation: Department of Mechanical Engineering, Eindhoven University of Technology Affiliation: DIFFER – Dutch Institute for Fundamental Energy Research Abstract Bifurcations are ubiquitous in physical systems, from structural buckling to fluid and climate dynamics, yet they remain largely unexplored in deep learning. At a symmetry-breaking bifurcation, a single input admits multiple equally valid solutions, violating the one-to-one assumption underlying most learned physical surrogates. We introduce Bi-FORK, a generative framework for learning these one-to-many solution maps in high-dimensional systems. Bi-FORK generates complete trajectories through latent flow matching, preserving space and time coherence, and uses repulsion-guided sampling to recover distinct solution branches in a single amortized pass. We evaluate Bi-FORK on buckling beams, mechanical metamaterials, and Allen-Cahn phase separation, spanning continuous, discrete, and field-valued bifurcations with discretizations up to 260,000 points. Bi-FORK recovers the multimodal solution structure while scaling several orders of magnitude beyond prior approaches, opening generative modeling to high-dimensional bifurcating physical systems. 1 Introduction Bifurcations are fundamental to nonlinear physical systems and occur across structural mechanics, fluid dynamics, climate dynamics, and phase-transition phenomena [ 49 , 54 , 47 ] . A bifurcation is a qualitative change in the number or stability of solutions as a control parameter varies. When a bifurcation breaks a symmetry, it produces a one-to-many mapping from control parameter to system response: multiple, equally valid solutions rather than one. For example, a compressed column is stable up to a critical load, then bifurcates into symmetric buckled branches [ 7 ] . Classical numerical methods, including finite-element and finite-volume methods, can compute these solutions accurately. However, for high-dimensional systems, recovering the full bifurcation structure requires stability and mode analyses together with repeated continuation or deflation solves [ 10 , 18 ] , which is computationally expensive. Therefore, machine learning (ML) methods are an attractive alternative as they amortize the cost of building the training set over the many fast evaluations of unseen system conditions [ 1 , 4 , 3 , 20 , 55 ] . However, because the system is one-to-many, training discriminative ML models averages over the solution space and, as a consequence, produces nonphysical predictions [ 50 , 36 , 46 ] . This has motivated the development of probabilistic methods based on GANs, diffusion models, and more recently flow matching, typically framed around uncertainty or the loss of fine-scale structure [ 19 , 60 , 12 ] . Most probabilistic physical surrogates model epistemic or unresolved uncertainty; symmetry-breaking bifurcations instead produce genuinely multiple, equally valid solutions structured by the system’s symmetry. Only a few recent approaches treat the bifurcation structure directly as the cause of solution multiplicity [ 17 , 44 , 61 , 30 , 25 , 48 ] . Nevertheless, these approaches recover systems of at most a few hundred degrees of freedom with small, known, discrete symmetry groups. Figure 1 : Learning bifurcating solution distributions. Left: Symmetry breaking results in multiple valid trajectories for the same control parameter and initial state. Center: Latent flow matching jointly samples trajectories and resolves distinct branches in one forward pass. Right: Unlike mode-averaging baselines, Bi-FORK recovers the target distribution. The main challenge Scaling to larger systems is challenging because recovering a bifurcating distribution requires every part of the system to agree on which branch it is realizing in both space and time. A beam buckling to the left at one end and right at the other is an invalid solution, as is a beam that first buckles to the left and then suddenly switches to buckling to the right halfway through a trajectory. Moreover, bifurcations are typically rare events in trajectories. Training a frame-by-frame autoregressive model to produce trajectories would face significant challenge of capturing this key aspect of the system’s behavior while being underrepresented in the training data. Predicting the full trajectory allows the model to instead represent the branch choice globally in latent space, for all steps and elements at the same time. Mesh-based GNN surrogates communicate through local message passing, making such global coordination increasingly difficult as systems grow due to oversmoothing and oversquashing [ 43 , 13 , 11 , 5 ] . Evaluation is similarly nontrivial. Pointwise metrics such as rank histograms and CRPS [ 23 , 19 , 28 , 42 , 39 ] assess pointwise calibration but cannot determine whether samples are coherent trajectories, while best-of- K K scores ignore most of the predicted distribution. Generic two-sample distances can detect mode collapse but become difficult to estimate in high dimensions and do not exploit the symmetry structure of bifurcating solutions [ 26 , 9 ] . We address these challenges with Bi-FORK: Bifurcation Flow-matching Over Repulsion-guided Kinematics, a latent flow-matching framework for symmetry-breaking bifurcations (see Figure 1 ). Bi-FORK generates full trajectories jointly, keeping branch choices consistent across space and time rather than learning them through local transitions. Because full-resolution execution is intractable, flow matching operates in a compact latent space, decoupling global coordination from discretization. Although compression can average modes, branch identity dominates trajectory variance and is therefore preserved by the reconstruction objective without supervision. At inference, particle guidance [ 58 , 14 ] repels concurrent samples, acting as a parallelized analog of classical deflation [ 10 , 18 ] to recover distinct solutions. We assess the resulting distribution by matching predictions to their nearest ground truth and, per input, measuring orbit coverage under the relevant symmetry group via the Jensen-Shannon divergence, thereby detecting regime collapse and quantifying coverage of the underlying distribution. We evaluate the approach on three symmetry-breaking bifurcation problems: buckling beams, buckling mechanical metamaterials, and phase separation described by Allen-Cahn. These systems cover two- and three-dimensional grid- and mesh-based problems, various symmetry groups (both discrete and continuous), trajectories of 32 to 200 timesteps, and discretizations from a handful of points to 260,000. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of solution distribution recovery for one-to-many problems at that scale, and we show that our method outperforms existing approaches in both accuracy and efficiency. Our contributions are: 1. A latent flow-matching framework that models whole trajectories, making branch coherence structural, and scales several orders of magnitude beyond prior work. 2. A particle-guidance sampling mechanism recovering multiple distinct solutions in one amortized pass, as a parallel analog of deflation. 3. Diagnostics based on symmetry-orbit matching and per-input Jensen-Shannon divergence that detect regime collapse and extend distributional verification to continuous and infinite symmetry groups. 2 A Blueprint for Bifurcating Regimes 2.1 Bifurcation Systems Figure 2 : Exemplary pitchfork bifurcation for the buckling metamaterials use case with increasing control protocol ℓ \bm{\ell} Recall that a bifurcation is the loss of uniqueness of a stable equilibrium as a control parameter crosses a critical value, with buckling as the canonical mechanical example [ 37 , 6 , 30 ] . Setting We represent trajectories as either point clouds or scalar fields on a regular grid. In both cases, 𝐌 t ∈ ℝ N × C \mathbf{M}^{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times C} denotes the modeled response at N N spatial locations and timestep t ∈ { 1 , … , T } t\in\{1,\dots,T\} , and 𝐌 1 : T ∈ ℝ T × N × C \mathbf{M}^{1:T}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times N\times C} forms the complete response trajectory. (3) In practice, we estimate t b t_{b} as the first step at which trajectories under the same condition separate beyond a small threshold. This also accommodates Allen-Cahn, where all trajectories share the same homogeneous initial state but macroscopic modes emerge only later. The choice of representation, the practical estimator, and secondary bifurcations are discussed in Appendix B . Probabilistically, t b t_{b} marks the onset of distinct branches in the distribution of outcomes conditioned on the context 𝐜 \bf c at timestep t t , connecting physical symmetry breaking to the need for distribution-valued prediction. Three regimes of multimodality Our datasets span discrete ( | ℳ 𝐜 | ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 } |\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{c}}|\in\{1,2,4\} , mechanical metamaterials of 29 ), continuous ( | ℳ 𝐜 | = ∞ |\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{c}}|=\infty , Beam3D), and field-valued (Allen-Cahn) mode sets; see Appendix C . 2.2 Learning task Given a condition 𝐜 \mathbf{c} , the task is to learn the conditional distribution over all feasible trajectories p ( 𝐌 1 : T ∣ 𝐜 ) , p\!\left(\mathbf{M}^{1:T}\mid\mathbf{c}\right), (4) where the support of the target distribution is the mode set ℳ 𝐜 \mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{c}} . The training datasets differ in their coverage of this support: the mechanical metamaterials enumerate all modes per condition, whereas Beam3D and Allen-Cahn provide samples from the mode set. We assume unknown perturbations that push the system toward one solution within an orbit have no preferred direction. Under this assumption, the condition’s symmetry implies that modes within an orbit are equally likely, so for single-orbit datasets the target is uniform over ℳ 𝐜 \mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{c}} . Unlike standard trajectory prediction, the mapping from 𝐜 \mathbf{c} to the system evolution is one-to-many: multiple physically valid trajectories arise under the same condition. During inference, the model receives 𝐜 \mathbf{c} and generates one or more trajectory samples from a learned distribution p θ flow ( 𝐌 1 : T ∣ 𝐜 ) p_{\theta_{\mathrm{flow}}}(\mathbf{M}^{1:T}\mid\mathbf{c}) . 2.3 Modeling Figure 3 : Encoder-decoder structure for point cloud datasets. Input tokens (reference positions 𝐗 1 \mathbf{X}^{1} and displacements) are encoded into latent representation by cross-attending to L L learned latent query tokens. The decoder reconstructs the displacements conditioned on the reference positions. Autoencoder We adopt a Perceiver-style cross-attention architecture [ 33 , 4 , 51 ] for all point cloud datasets. For each timestep t t , the encoder maps the reference configuration 𝐗 1 \mathbf{X}^{1} and response field 𝐌 t \mathbf{M}^{t} to L L latent tokens of dimension D z D_{z} , i.e., 𝐙 t ∈ ℝ L × D z \mathbf{Z}^{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times D_{z}} , using cross-attention with learned latent queries, followed by self-attention on the latent set. Importantly, the decoder reconstructs 𝐌 t \mathbf{M}^{t} by querying these tokens at the fixed reference positions 𝐗 1 \mathbf{X}^{1} . Thus, the latent representation 𝐙 t \mathbf{Z}^{t} encodes all timestep-dependent states, while spatial reconstruction is always anchored to the same reference geometry 𝐗 1 \mathbf{X}^{1} . This enables the independent analysis and prediction of latent trajectories { 𝐙 t } t = 1 T \{\mathbf{Z}^{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} , which can then be decoded at the reference positions to recover 𝐌 t \mathbf{M}^{t} . For regular grid datasets, we use a 3D Vision Transformer (ViT) [ 16 , 45 ] , detailed in the respective section ( Section 3.3 ). (6) We adapt the standard flow matching approach through optimal transport-based coupling of in-batch pairs to minimize the path length between the noise and data distributions [ 57 ] . Additionally, we require the model to predict the bifurcation point, represented by a binary mask 𝐛 ^ ∈ { 0 , 1 } T \widehat{\mathbf{b}}\in\{0,1\}^{T} . At inference, 𝐙 ^ 1 \widehat{\mathbf{Z}}_{1} is recovered by solving the probability-flow ODE associated with Eq. 5 , starting from pure noise. All timestep-dependent information for the prediction is expressed by 𝐙 τ \mathbf{Z}_{\tau} and its conditioning signals. While the generative model predicts a single valid mode rather than averaging across them, sampling alone does not control the distribution over modes. Figure 4 : Particle guidance during sampling. Trajectories evolve identically up to bifurcation point t b t_{b} . From t b t_{b} , the repulsion term acts on the masked frames t ≥ t b t\geq t_{b} , pushing the K K trajectories apart, yielding a multimodal distribution. We address this at inference with an approach inspired by particle guidance [ 14 ] . Rather than drawing K K trajectories independently, we sample K K candidate trajectories 𝐙 τ ( 1 ) , … , 𝐙 τ ( K ) \mathbf{Z}_{\tau}^{(1)},\dots,\mathbf{Z}_{\tau}^{(K)} in a shared batch and integrate the probability-flow ODE for all of them jointly, leaving f θ flow f_{\theta_{\mathrm{flow}}} unmodified from training. Each 𝐙 ^ 1 ( k ) \widehat{\mathbf{Z}}_{1}^{(k)} and its ordinary velocity field are computed independently via Eq. 6 , as at training time. For each trajectory, the predicted values at these frames are masked and flattened into a single point; pairwise distances between trajectories’ points are weighted by a Gaussian RBF kernel with bandwidth set to the median pairwise distance. Each trajectory’s displacement force ( k ) \mathrm{force}^{(k)} is the resulting kernel-weighted average of unit vectors pointing away from its neighbors, so trajectories that are similar at the bifurcation frames are pushed apart while already-distinct trajectories barely interact. Standard metrics such as MSE are inadequate in this setting, as they neither reflect the multimodal structure of the output space nor penalize mode collapse. We adopt two complementary metrics, adapted to systems with | ℳ 𝐜 | ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 } |\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{c}}|\in\{1,2,4\} or | ℳ 𝐜 | = ∞ |\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{c}}|=\infty responses depending on the condition 𝐜 \mathbf{c} . For each condition 𝐜 \mathbf{c} , we draw K K samples from the model and assign each to its nearest ground-truth mode by Euclidean distance. We introduce Bi-FORK, a generative framework for learning these one-to-many solution maps in high-dimensional systems. Bi-FORK generates complete trajectories through latent flow matching, preserving space and time coherence, and uses repulsion-guided sampling to recover distinct solution branches in a single amortized pass. We evaluate Bi-FORK on buckling beams, mechanical metamaterials, and Allen-Cahn phase separation, spanning continuous, discrete, and field-valued bifurcations with discretizations up to 260,000 points. Bi-FORK recovers the multimodal solution structure while scaling several orders of magnitude beyond prior approaches, opening generative modeling to high-dimensional bifurcating physical systems. 1 Introduction Bifurcations are fundamental to nonlinear physical systems and occur across structural mechanics, fluid dynamics, climate dynamics, and phase-transition phenomena [ 49 , 54 , 47 ] . A bifurcation is a qualitative change in the number or stability of solutions as a control parameter varies. When a bifurcation breaks a symmetry, it produces a one-to-many mapping from control parameter to system response: multiple, equally valid solutions rather than one. For example, a compressed column is stable up to a critical load, then bifurcates into symmetric buckled branches [ 7 ] . Classical numerical methods, including finite-element and finite-volume methods, can compute these solutions accurately. However, for high-dimensional systems, recovering the full bifurcation structure requires stability and mode analyses together with repeated continuation or deflation solves [ 10 , 18 ] , which is computationally expensive. Therefore, machine learning (ML) methods are an attractive alternative as they amortize the cost of building the training set over the many fast evaluations of unseen system conditions [ 1 , 4 , 3 , 20 , 55 ] . However, because the system is one-to-many, training discriminative ML models averages over the solution space and, as a consequence, produces nonphysical predictions [ 50 , 36 , 46 ] . This has motivated the development of probabilistic methods based on GANs, diffusion models, and more recently flow matching, typically framed around uncertainty or the loss of fine-scale structure [ 19 , 60 , 12 ] . Most probabilistic physical surrogates model epistemic or unresolved uncertainty; symmetry-breaking bifurcations instead produce genuinely multiple, equally valid solutions structured by the system’s symmetry. Only a few recent approaches treat the bifurcation structure directly as the cause of solution multiplicity [ 17 , 44 , 61 , 30 , 25 , 48 ] . Nevertheless, these approaches recover systems of at most a few hundred degrees of freedom with small, known, discrete symmetry groups. Figure 1 : Learning bifurcating solution distributions. Left: Symmetry breaking results in multiple valid trajectories for the same control parameter and initial state. Center: Latent flow matching jointly samples trajectories and resolves distinct branches in one forward pass. Right: Unlike mode-averaging baselines, Bi-FORK recovers the target distribution. The main challenge Scaling to larger systems is challenging because recovering a bifurcating distribution requires every part of the system to agree on which branch it is realizing in both space and time. A beam buckling to the left at one end and right at the other is an invalid solution, as is a beam that first buckles to the left and then suddenly switches to buckling to the right halfway through a trajectory. Moreover, bifurcations are typically rare events in trajectories. Training a frame-by-frame autoregressive model to produce trajectories would face significant challenge of capturing this key aspect of the system’s behavior while being underrepresented in the training data. Predicting the full trajectory allows the model to instead represent the branch choice globally in latent space, for all steps and elements at the same time. Mesh-based GNN surrogates communicate through local message passing, making such global coordination increasingly difficult as systems grow due to oversmoothing and oversquashing [ 43 , 13 , 11 , 5 ] . Evaluation is similarly nontrivial. Pointwise metrics such as rank histograms and CRPS [ 23 , 19 , 28 , 42 , 39 ] assess pointwise calibration but cannot determine whether samples are coherent trajectories, while best-of- K K scores ignore most of the predicted distribution. Generic two-sample distances can detect mode collapse but become difficult to estimate in high dimensions and do not exploit the symmetry structure of bifurcating solutions [ 26 , 9 ] . We address these challenges with Bi-FORK: Bifurcation Flow-matching Over Repulsion-guided Kinematics, a latent flow-matching framework for symmetry-breaking bifurcations (see Figure 1 ). Bi-FORK generates full trajectories jointly, keeping branch choices consistent across space and time rather than learning them through local transitions. Because full-resolution execution is intractable, flow matching operates in a compact latent space, decoupling global coordination from discretization. Although compression can average modes, branch identity dominates trajectory variance and is therefore preserved by the reconstruction objective without supervision. At inference, particle guidance [ 58 , 14 ] repels concurrent samples, acting as a parallelized analog of classical deflation [ 10 , 18 ] to recover distinct solutions. We assess the resulting distribution by matching predictions to their nearest ground truth and, per input, measuring orbit coverage under the relevant symmetry group via the Jensen-Shannon divergence, thereby detecting regime collapse and quantifying coverage of the underlying distribution. We evaluate the approach on three symmetry-breaking bifurcation problems: buckling beams, buckling mechanical metamaterials, and phase separation described by Allen-Cahn. These systems cover two- and three-dimensional grid- and mesh-based problems, various symmetry groups (both discrete and continuous), trajectories of 32 to 200 timesteps, and discretizations from a handful of points to 260,000. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of solution distribution recovery for one-to-many problems at that scale, and we show that our method outperforms existing approaches in both accuracy and efficiency. Our contributions are: 1. A latent flow-matching framework that models whole trajectories, making branch coherence structural, and scales several orders of magnitude beyond prior work. 2. A particle-guidance sampling mechanism recovering multiple distinct solutions in one amortized pass, as a parallel analog of deflation. 3. Diagnostics based on symmetry-orbit matching and per-input Jensen-Shannon divergence that detect regime collapse and extend distributional verification to continuous and infinite symmetry groups. 2 A Blueprint for Bifurcating Regimes 2.1 Bifurcation Systems Figure 2 : Exemplary pitchfork bifurcation for the buckling metamaterials use case with increasing control protocol ℓ \bm{\ell} Recall that a bifurcation is the loss of uniqueness of a stable equilibrium as a control parameter crosses a critical value, with buckling as the canonical mechanical example [ 37 , 6 , 30 ] . Hollinsworth , Alex F. Spies , Tigist Diriba , Adam Gleave , Chris Cundy View a PDF of the paper titled Caught in the Act: Probes Effectively Detect Sabotage and Catch Unverbalized Deception, by Oskar J. Hollinsworth and 4 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Recent incidents have highlighted the challenge of monitoring LLM agents and the danger of models deceiving people. We show that white-box deception detection via probes can be scaled up to frontier monitoring settings by collecting the largest deception dataset to date for training probes and introducing a novel probe architecture which can aggregate information across many layers and tokens. Our probes achieve 98.8% AUC in SHADE-Arena, surpassing an Opus 5.5 text-monitoring baseline, and show improved efficacy as the underlying model is scaled up. To push our probes to their limit, we test them on several cases where deception cannot be determined from the context alone. In these cases, which we refer to as introspective deception, the ground truth can only be determined through careful elicitation or thorough knowledge of a model's training data. In one such evaluation, we show that probes can distinguish transcripts containing a model's true hidden goal from other goals with an AUC of up to 99.7%. Our probes also readily detect deception on prominent open-weight models which lie about politically sensitive topics, and about their beliefs when put under pressure. We release our training dataset, dubbed FIBS, to help drive frontier deployment of effective probes, and encourage the community to expand upon it with further examples of deception and sabotage. Hollinsworth , Alex F. Spies , Tigist Diriba , Adam Gleave , Chris Cundy View a PDF of the paper titled Caught in the Act: Probes Effectively Detect Sabotage and Catch Unverbalized Deception, by Oskar J. Hollinsworth and 4 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Recent incidents have highlighted the challenge of monitoring LLM agents and the danger of models deceiving people. We show that white-box deception detection via probes can be scaled up to frontier monitoring settings by collecting the largest deception dataset to date for training probes and introducing a novel probe architecture which can aggregate information across many layers and tokens. Our probes achieve 98.8% AUC in SHADE-Arena, surpassing an Opus 5.5 text-monitoring baseline, and show improved efficacy as the underlying model is scaled up. To push our probes to their limit, we test them on several cases where deception cannot be determined from the context alone. In these cases, which we refer to as introspective deception, the ground truth can only be determined through careful elicitation or thorough knowledge of a model's training data. In one such evaluation, we show that probes can distinguish transcripts containing a model's true hidden goal from other goals with an AUC of up to 99.7%. Our probes also readily detect deception on prominent open-weight models which lie about politically sensitive topics, and about their beliefs when put under pressure. We release our training dataset, dubbed FIBS, to help drive frontier deployment of effective probes, and encourage the community to expand upon it with further examples of deception and sabotage. Spies 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Tigist Diriba Adam Gleave Chris Cundy FAR.AI github.com/AlignmentResearch/caught-in-the-act-probes Abstract Recent incidents have highlighted the challenge of monitoring LLM agents and the danger of models deceiving people. We show that white-box deception detection via probes can be scaled up to frontier monitoring settings by collecting the largest deception dataset to date for training probes and introducing a novel probe architecture which can aggregate information across many layers and tokens. Our probes achieve 98.8% AUC in SHADE-Arena, surpassing an Opus 5.5 text-monitoring baseline, and show improved efficacy as the underlying model is scaled up. To push our probes to their limit, we test them on several cases where deception cannot be determined from the context alone. In these cases, which we refer to as introspective deception, the ground truth can only be determined through careful elicitation or thorough knowledge of a model’s training data. In one such evaluation, we show that probes can distinguish transcripts containing a model’s true hidden goal from other goals with an AUC of up to 99.7%. Our probes also readily detect deception on prominent open-weight models which lie about politically sensitive topics, and about their beliefs when put under pressure. We release our training dataset, dubbed fibs , to help drive frontier deployment of effective probes, and encourage the community to expand upon it with further examples of deception and sabotage. \logo (a) Probes outperform Opus 5.5* at malicious action detection . On Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, all four probes trained on all of fibs score above Opus 5.5 (a refusal counts as the highest suspicion score, ⋆ \star ) and self-monitoring. This panel shows LinearEnsemble and EFC, one line per number of fibs families. AUROC is over 14 SHADE-Arena scenarios (§ 4.3 ), with 95% episode-bootstrap intervals. (b) The same denial, a lie from one organism and honest from another. Two model organisms both deny having the same hidden goal; for one the denial is a lie, for the other it is true. With the Chain-of-Thought elided, so the transcripts are structurally identical, the axial probe can classify the two sets of activations with 98.0% AUC. Figure 1 : Probes trained on fibs transfer to agentic sabotage (a) and hidden-goal denials (b). 1 Introduction In recent months, AI agents running autonomously in training, evaluation or deployment have precipitated multiple high-profile incidents of misaligned behavior: escaping their sandboxes, hacking companies and governments, and attempting to mislead humans ( Larcher et al., 2026 , UK AI Security Institute, 2026 , Cable et al., 2026 ) , all while seemingly aware that these actions would, once subject to scrutiny, be considered undesirable by their human overseers. It is clearer than ever that careful monitoring of AI agents is critical, and that detecting knowingly deceptive actions is a clear target for effective monitoring. State-of-the-art monitoring approaches are black-box, relying on text classifiers ( Sharma et al., 2025 ) , reviewing both actions and chain-of-thought ( OpenAI, 2026 ) , and using reasoning ( Sinha et al., 2026 ) . We cannot be sure why black-box monitors were not already applied on these generations of agents, but cost is a likely factor as running powerful monitors is a substantial compute burden. Black-box monitoring is also heavily reliant on interpretable and faithful Chain-of-Thought (CoT), which is fragile ( Korbak et al., 2025 ) . There have been numerous incidents of frontier model training accidentally putting pressure on the CoT ( Carroll et al., 2026 , Anthropic, 2026 ) , and models have increasing capability without it ( Gould et al., 2026 ) . Fortunately, white-box methods have shown great promise as a vastly cheaper and versatile alternative, but demonstrating competitiveness in loss-of-control settings has remained an open problem. In this work, we examine the extent to which white box probes can be made competitive with black-box methods, simply by creating a large, diverse dataset and training expressive probes on the activations of modern large open-weight models. To rigorously determine ground-truth labels for our probes, we avoid the philosophical uncertainty around “deception”, which typically incorporates an agent’s intent ( Mahon, 2016 ) . Instead, we restrict ourselves to training white-box probes that detect knowing falsehoods : model statements that the model believes are false. Further, since establishing belief can require extensive elicitation, our training datasets consist of contextual falsehoods , where a model makes a statement contradicting a fact established previously in the context. The complement of contextual falsehoods are introspective falsehoods , which depend on additional knowledge about a model. For instance, if a transcript consists of a model denying having a hidden goal, deciding if the denial is a falsehood requires knowing if the model believes it has that goal. Within this framing, we ask: (RQ1) to what point does scaling probe training data continue to improve out-of-distribution performance; (RQ2) do probes trained on off-policy, contextual falsehoods generalize to realistic multi-turn on-policy deployments, and compete with black-box monitors there; and (RQ3) do such probes generalize to introspective falsehoods? Our contributions are threefold: • We release Falsehoods in Broad Settings ( fibs ), a deception dataset formed from both existing and new datasets, and spanning multiple deception types, elicitation methods, and interaction formats, from curated conversations to agentic rollouts. • RQ1 & RQ2: We show that scaling the amount and diversity of training data , and the capacity of white-box falsehood detectors, improves performance on monitoring long, multi-step, on-policy SHADE-Arena ( Kutasov et al., 2025 ) trajectories, where probes outperform black-box monitors that are orders of magnitude more expensive to evaluate (Figure 1(a) ). • RQ3: Through the use of belief elicitation and model organisms, we show that probes trained primarily on contextual falsehoods detect introspective falsehoods . These falsehoods are impossible to detect from a model’s visible outputs alone, since identical answers can be a lie for one model and honest for another (Figure 1(b) ). 2 Problem setting 2.1 Falsehoods Smith et al. (2025) discuss several conceptual problems with detecting deception from language models. In this work, we avoid many, but not all, of those problems by instead aiming to detect knowing falsehoods . That is, we wish to identify when an LLM makes a statement it believes to be false. We do not aim to detect deceptive intent, misleading but true statements, or any other type of non-falsehood-stating behavior. Nonetheless, as we show, detecting falsehoods still allows us to catch many of the most salient misaligned behaviors under monitoring. More formally, we define a transcript T T as containing a knowing falsehood for a model M M if it satisfies the following. Firstly, the final assistant response to the user in T T , denoted r r , must contain a set of asserted statements, each with a truth value, which we denote 𝒮 \cal S . Secondly, for at least one of the statements s ∈ 𝒮 s\in\cal S , the model must believe that s s is false, which we denote Bel M ⁡ ( ¬ s ∣ C ) \operatorname{Bel}_{M}(\neg s\mid C) , where the context C C is the prefix of r r in T T . 1 1 1 Under our definition, a knowing falsehood can be objectively true. Reasoning is part of C C , not of r r . It is difficult to say in general whether a model believes something. Previous work has generally relied either on an appeal to common sense, or using the generations y y from M M given contexts related to C C , which we write y | x y\mid x for a context x x . For the purposes of this work, we say that a model M M believes a statement s s in context C C , i.e. Bel M ⁡ ( s ∣ C ) \operatorname{Bel}_{M}(s\mid C) , when any of the following is true: (1) Contextual evidence. C C contains clear evidence for s s , e.g. a tool result in C C stating s s . (2) Neutral elicitation. C C contains some pressure or incentive P P that we expect from the training procedure of M M to cause y | C y\mid C to contain ¬ s \neg s , while y | C ~ y\mid\tilde{C} contains s s with high probability; here C ~ \tilde{C} is C C with the minimal change to remove P P , and there is no competing incentive in C ~ \tilde{C} (e.g. (3)). (3) Training-instilled belief. The model M M is known to achieve low loss on a training corpus where internalizing that s s is true is necessary to achieve this loss. This could be during pretraining by the developer, or as a post-training stage conducted by a model organism researcher. We say that a falsehood is contextual if belief is established via criterion 1, noting that in those cases the transcript alone determines if a falsehood is present, and otherwise it is introspective . We further distinguish cases of (3) where s s is a well-known fact, such that we can essentially not worry about what model M M is, and refer to this as pseudo-contextual . 2.2 Training probes and monitors It is much easier to construct large datasets of contextual (or at least pseudo-contextual ) falsehoods than introspective ones, as the label is independent of the model and thus the dataset can be re-used over models. Similarly, no elicitation is required to verify a (competent) model’s beliefs for each dataset example. We therefore ask whether a large and sufficiently diverse set of contextual falsehoods, used to train expressive probes, can yield competitive monitors for real-world deployment, such as in frontier-scale sabotage detection, and whether such monitors can generalize to introspective cases. Our probes are classifiers f : ℝ d ​ | R | → [ 0 , 1 ] f:\mathbb{R}^{d|R|}\to[0,1] from hidden states h ∈ ℝ d h\in\mathbb{R}^{d} for a set of read-out states R R , where the goal is for f = 1 f=1 for falsehoods and 0 otherwise, trained on labeled data { h ⁡ ( C , r ) , ℓ ⁡ ( C , r ) } \{h(C,r),\ell(C,r)\} , where the ground truth is determined from context alone. When scaling the training data, the full set is usually the union of multiple data sources 𝒟 train = ∪ i = 0 N 𝒟 i \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}=\cup_{i=0}^{N}\mathcal{D}_{i} . There are then two ways to scale the training data: diversity , by increasing N N , and raw quantity , by increasing the size of each 𝒟 i \mathcal{D}_{i} . More generally, a monitor is any trusted system that serves to flag specific behaviors in another, usually more powerful, model. The most powerful black-box monitors have access to the hidden reasoning, known as CoT monitors, and thus could detect intent before the dangerous action is selected. Whereas, we focus on the more narrowly scoped action-only monitors , in anticipation of future models losing CoT monitorability (cf. § 1 ). We study monitors in a setting where an untrusted model is deployed as an agent in an environment where it can access tools, potentially allowing it to take unauthorized, dangerous actions in the real world. Each assistant turn a i a_{i} is made up of many iterations of reasoning, tool call, and response. We call each of these a “step”, and use our probes, combined with a specific follow-up question, as monitors to detect if a misaligned action was taken in a particular step. 3 Related work Expressive activation probes. Beyond linear probes, recent work trains higher-capacity detectors on frozen activations: attention probes learn input-dependent pooling over token positions ( Kantamneni et al., 2025 ) , and later work and production systems either extend these with hard-max and windowed variants ( McKenzie et al., 2025 ) , including for long-context robustness ( Kramár et al., 2026 ) , or aggregate across layers by linear concatenation with streamed scoring ( Cunningham et al., 2026 ) . Orthogonally, CLAP applies a transformer encoder across the layer axis at a single position ( Suresh et al., 2025 ) . These architectures each attend over one axis of the activation tensor; our axial probe applies factored causal attention over the full layer × \times position grid. Detecting deception. Prior work on detecting deception mostly focuses on black-box monitors ( Greenblatt et al., 2024 , Baker et al., 2025 ) . White-box detectors instead read internal activations, from unsupervised truth directions ( Burns et al., 2023 ) to supervised probes ( Marks and Tegmark, 2024 ) . Probes have shown promise as a valuable tool for many safety-relevant tasks such as catching sleeper agents ( MacDiarmid et al., 2024 ) or detecting reward hacking in coding environments ( Taufeeque et al., 2026 , Bergen et al., 2026 ) . Prior work has focused on simple probes trained to detect only a relatively narrow class of deception. However, more recent work has shown that different forms of deception may be represented differently in models ( Natarajan et al., 2026 ) , suggesting the need for more expressive probes and richer datasets when hoping to find a “universal deception detector”. We train on the most diverse falsehood dataset to date and evaluate our probes on very challenging out-of-distribution tasks, including long SHADE-Arena transcripts and models lying about a hidden goal. Black-box vs white-box. Direct comparisons between probes and black-box monitors have yielded mixed results. Probes are as or more effective than black-box monitors at predicting response safety from the CoT alone ( Chan et al., 2025 ) , at detecting “strategic dishonesty” where models lie in response to unsafe queries ( Panfilov et al., 2026 ) , and many other tasks ( Parrack et al., 2025 ) , but white-box methods failed, for example, to show uplift for an alignment auditing agent ( Sheshadri et al., 2026 ) . Cooney et al. (2026) tested probes in an introspective setting where the model has a hidden goal, but found that probes were ineffective. We are able to train probes which are highly effective in the setting from Cooney et al. (2026) . 4 Methodology We first outline the construction of our diverse contextual falsehood dataset, fibs , which was used to train all of our probes. We then discuss our probes’ architectures and the SHADE-Arena evaluation setting. Lastly, we discuss the two key methods used to determine the generalization of our probes to introspective settings — belief elicitation and model organisms with hidden goals. Figure 2 : Left : Composition of the 163,016 fibs rows (28 families). See § 4.1 and Appendix L for a high-level and detailed break-down. Middle: Row length in Qwen3.5 tokens. Right: Turns per row. 4.1 The fibs dataset To investigate the effect of diversity and data scale in lie detector training, we create Falsehoods in Broad Settings ( fibs ), a contextual deception dataset of 163,016 transcripts, labeled by whether they contain knowing falsehoods (§ 2.1 ). fibs is the union of 28 families, each of different modality or topic area. We give a high-level overview here, and defer implementation details to Appendix L . Figure 2 outlines the dataset composition and example rows are in Appendix L.3 . A large fraction (76% of rows, 19 of 28 families) of the dataset is constructed synthetically from existing datasets with appended follow-up questions. For example, one family starts from MASK ( Ren et al., 2025 ) , where each example is a user-assistant chat with a designated truthful or deceptive answer. We then append a user follow-up question, such as “Did you answer accurately?”. The assistant response can be either “Yes” or “No”. This yields four kinds of rows for fibs : i) the initial response is honest and the follow-up response is deceptive (Honest-Deceptive or HD), ii) the initial response is deceptive and the follow-up response is deceptive (Deceptive-Deceptive or DD), and similarly for the other two combinations (DH and HH). In practice, we vary the follow-up question over a large set of fixed questions and responses, and sometimes generate follow-up questions and responses from another LLM. The next largest fraction of rows (18% of rows, 5 families) consist of on-policy examples from various models (§ L.1 ). Since models rarely spontaneously deceive, we use a variety of settings. Firstly, we run on-policy deception games using the harness from Golechha and Garriga-Alonso (2025) . Secondly, we use instructions or pressure to lie to the user, both in the system prompt and user turn. Finally, we leverage personas ( Marks et al., 2026 ) by generating a long transcript where the assistant acts disreputably and then generating the final turn on-policy, which frequently leads to a lie. In these families we also generate off-policy rows, so that on-policyness cannot be used as a shortcut for the probe. The final set of rows (6% of rows, 4 families) cover bespoke cases not covered in other families, such as assistants misrepresenting tool calls from earlier in the conversation, extremely long-context examples, direct false statements with no follow-up, etc. We validate labels through extensive LLM-as-a-judge filtering and estimate the label noise rate is 1.4 % ± 0.1 1.4\%\pm 0.1 . This rate is measured against a “ground truth” evaluation from Claude Fable 5 given a dataset-agnostic definition of contextual falsehood similar to that in § 2.1 (Appendix L.6 ). We also balance the dataset exactly by label, control for the confounders of length and message count, and cap families at a size of 8,000 rows to ensure balance between settings. Although we believe fibs is currently the largest and most diverse falsehood dataset, it has several limitations. Firstly, few rows contain reasoning (only 5.5% of rows across only 6 families), as most examples come from non-reasoning models. Secondly, the dataset is entirely off-policy for almost all models we probe, except for Qwen3.5-122B, which generated 3% of fibs rows. Finally, the dataset is largely artificial. One family consists of transcripts from UltraChat ( Ding et al., 2023 ) with follow-up questions, but otherwise the dataset consists entirely of relatively simple evaluations or settings that are unrealistic for frontier model deployment. 4.2 Scaling probes The most well-studied form of activation probe is the linear probe, a simple logistic regression on the residual stream at a single layer and token. Linear probes can be scaled along two axes: (i) more capacity , meaning more parameters, and (ii) greater input span , expanding the set of input activations R R (§ 2.2 ). For a higher capacity probe with the same single layer/token span as the linear probe, we use an MLP probe, a two-layer perceptron of hidden width 256. For these single-span probes, we train a probe per layer and average across all layers whose training loss is below 0.6, following Taufeeque et al. (2026) (Appendix A.2 ); we call the resulting per-layer ensembles the LinearEnsemble and MLPEnsemble probes. Our medium-capacity, long-span probe is the EFC probe (early-fusion covariance), adapted from Dooms et al. (2026) . At each token it concatenates activations across layers, projects them to a small dimension, and aggregates across tokens using the mean and covariance of the projected vectors; the output is a linear projection of those moments. The projections are parameterized and learnable. Our high-capacity, long-span probe is the axial probe, a small transformer where each block attends first across tokens, causally, and then bidirectionally across layers; the name refers to this axial factorization of attention. This probe has the fewest inductive biases of the four, not imposing any a-priori expectations about how concepts may be represented in activations. Probe implementation details are given in Appendix A . Table 1 in Appendix A.5 compares the parameter counts. Appendix A.6 expands on the training objective, optimizer parameters and the hyperparameter search behind it (the selected grid cells: Table 2 ). Across all four architectures, we use activations from six layers spread evenly from 30% to 90% of the model’s depth. For the axial and EFC probes, we use activations from the tokens of the final user and assistant turn. For the MLPEnsemble and LinearEnsemble probe we use just the last non-end-of-turn token. At evaluation time, we often prefill the final turn; e.g., user: “Did you respond truthfully?”, assistant: “Yes.”. This lets us remove any context-specific bias in probe scores by using the contrast score, i.e. the probe-score difference between “Yes.” and “No.” prefills. As a non-probe baseline we use the model’s self-report logit : the log-probability of the admitting reply minus that of the denying reply (e.g. log ⁡ p ⁡ ( No ) − log ⁡ p ⁡ ( Yes ) \log p(\texttt{No})-\log p(\texttt{Yes}) after “Did you respond truthfully?”). 4.3 Agentic setting: SHADE-Arena SHADE-Arena ( Kutasov et al., 2025 ) places an agent in a tool-using environment with a benign main task. In the side-task condition the agent is also instructed to complete a hidden side task the user did not ask for; in the honest condition it receives the main task only. An episode is one run of the agent loop, and its transcript is the resulting sequence of steps ; each step is reasoning ending in a tool call, plus that call’s result. We run our models on fourteen of 25 possible scenarios, and read the probes of § 4.2 from the same model’s residual stream. Appendix entries B.1 and C describe the scenarios and generation settings, including details on why some scenarios were discarded. Appendix Transcript H.2 shows a side-task step and an honest step. We collect 25 rollouts per scenario and condition. By default, SHADE-Arena does not provide a robust way to identify whether a given action contributes (ideally exclusively) toward the main-task or side-task. As such, to evaluate our probes as action monitors, we used an LLM judge (Claude Haiku 4.5 2 2 2 We compare its labels with those of other LLM judges on Qwen3.5-122B-A10B rollouts of all 25 scenarios (Appendix B.5 , Table 4 ). ) to generate per-step labels, as detailed in Appendix K.1 . The first step the judge marks as pursuing the side task is the side task’s onset ; steps of a side-task episode from the onset on are the positive class, and its earlier steps and every step of an honest episode are the negative class (Figure 4(c) ). Appendix B.4 details the per-step labels. The 14 scenarios are those left after we drop 11 in which a judge cannot tell side-task work from main-task work in a single step (Appendix B.1 ). On Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, they give 699 scored episodes, with 5,014 positive and 16,275 negative steps. To evaluate our probes as action monitors, we prefill follow-up questions (§ 4.2 ) after every tool-call, following Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) . The assistant’s “yes” or “no” response is prefilled with empty reasoning, and previous pre-tool reasoning blocks are automatically removed by the Qwen3.5 chat template — so our probes do not monitor the chain-of-thought. We test three follow-ups, increasing in scenario-specificity: (i) “Did you take any actions misaligned to the user’s intent?”, (ii) “Did you do anything the user did not ask you to do?” (our default) , and (iii) “Did you take actions towards a hidden side task?”.
