Spies 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Tigist Diriba Adam Gleave Chris Cundy FAR.AI github.com/AlignmentResearch/caught-in-the-act-probes Abstract Recent incidents have highlighted the challenge of monitoring LLM agents and the danger of models deceiving people. We show that white-box deception detection via probes can be scaled up to frontier monitoring settings by collecting the largest deception dataset to date for training probes and introducing a novel probe architecture which can aggregate information across many layers and tokens. Our probes achieve 98.8% AUC in SHADE-Arena, surpassing an Opus 5.5 text-monitoring baseline, and show improved efficacy as the underlying model is scaled up. To push our probes to their limit, we test them on several cases where deception cannot be determined from the context alone. In these cases, which we refer to as introspective deception, the ground truth can only be determined through careful elicitation or thorough knowledge of a model’s training data. In one such evaluation, we show that probes can distinguish transcripts containing a model’s true hidden goal from other goals with an AUC of up to 99.7%. Our probes also readily detect deception on prominent open-weight models which lie about politically sensitive topics, and about their beliefs when put under pressure. We release our training dataset, dubbed fibs , to help drive frontier deployment of effective probes, and encourage the community to expand upon it with further examples of deception and sabotage. \logo (a) Probes outperform Opus 5.5* at malicious action detection . On Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, all four probes trained on all of fibs score above Opus 5.5 (a refusal counts as the highest suspicion score, ⋆ \star ) and self-monitoring. This panel shows LinearEnsemble and EFC, one line per number of fibs families. AUROC is over 14 SHADE-Arena scenarios (§ 4.3 ), with 95% episode-bootstrap intervals. (b) The same denial, a lie from one organism and honest from another. Two model organisms both deny having the same hidden goal; for one the denial is a lie, for the other it is true. With the Chain-of-Thought elided, so the transcripts are structurally identical, the axial probe can classify the two sets of activations with 98.0% AUC. Figure 1 : Probes trained on fibs transfer to agentic sabotage (a) and hidden-goal denials (b). 1 Introduction In recent months, AI agents running autonomously in training, evaluation or deployment have precipitated multiple high-profile incidents of misaligned behavior: escaping their sandboxes, hacking companies and governments, and attempting to mislead humans ( Larcher et al., 2026 , UK AI Security Institute, 2026 , Cable et al., 2026 ) , all while seemingly aware that these actions would, once subject to scrutiny, be considered undesirable by their human overseers. It is clearer than ever that careful monitoring of AI agents is critical, and that detecting knowingly deceptive actions is a clear target for effective monitoring. State-of-the-art monitoring approaches are black-box, relying on text classifiers ( Sharma et al., 2025 ) , reviewing both actions and chain-of-thought ( OpenAI, 2026 ) , and using reasoning ( Sinha et al., 2026 ) . We cannot be sure why black-box monitors were not already applied on these generations of agents, but cost is a likely factor as running powerful monitors is a substantial compute burden. Black-box monitoring is also heavily reliant on interpretable and faithful Chain-of-Thought (CoT), which is fragile ( Korbak et al., 2025 ) . There have been numerous incidents of frontier model training accidentally putting pressure on the CoT ( Carroll et al., 2026 , Anthropic, 2026 ) , and models have increasing capability without it ( Gould et al., 2026 ) . Fortunately, white-box methods have shown great promise as a vastly cheaper and versatile alternative, but demonstrating competitiveness in loss-of-control settings has remained an open problem. In this work, we examine the extent to which white box probes can be made competitive with black-box methods, simply by creating a large, diverse dataset and training expressive probes on the activations of modern large open-weight models. To rigorously determine ground-truth labels for our probes, we avoid the philosophical uncertainty around “deception”, which typically incorporates an agent’s intent ( Mahon, 2016 ) . Instead, we restrict ourselves to training white-box probes that detect knowing falsehoods : model statements that the model believes are false. Further, since establishing belief can require extensive elicitation, our training datasets consist of contextual falsehoods , where a model makes a statement contradicting a fact established previously in the context. The complement of contextual falsehoods are introspective falsehoods , which depend on additional knowledge about a model. For instance, if a transcript consists of a model denying having a hidden goal, deciding if the denial is a falsehood requires knowing if the model believes it has that goal. Within this framing, we ask: (RQ1) to what point does scaling probe training data continue to improve out-of-distribution performance; (RQ2) do probes trained on off-policy, contextual falsehoods generalize to realistic multi-turn on-policy deployments, and compete with black-box monitors there; and (RQ3) do such probes generalize to introspective falsehoods? Our contributions are threefold: • We release Falsehoods in Broad Settings ( fibs ), a deception dataset formed from both existing and new datasets, and spanning multiple deception types, elicitation methods, and interaction formats, from curated conversations to agentic rollouts. • RQ1 & RQ2: We show that scaling the amount and diversity of training data , and the capacity of white-box falsehood detectors, improves performance on monitoring long, multi-step, on-policy SHADE-Arena ( Kutasov et al., 2025 ) trajectories, where probes outperform black-box monitors that are orders of magnitude more expensive to evaluate (Figure 1(a) ). • RQ3: Through the use of belief elicitation and model organisms, we show that probes trained primarily on contextual falsehoods detect introspective falsehoods . These falsehoods are impossible to detect from a model’s visible outputs alone, since identical answers can be a lie for one model and honest for another (Figure 1(b) ). 2 Problem setting 2.1 Falsehoods Smith et al. (2025) discuss several conceptual problems with detecting deception from language models. In this work, we avoid many, but not all, of those problems by instead aiming to detect knowing falsehoods . That is, we wish to identify when an LLM makes a statement it believes to be false. We do not aim to detect deceptive intent, misleading but true statements, or any other type of non-falsehood-stating behavior. Nonetheless, as we show, detecting falsehoods still allows us to catch many of the most salient misaligned behaviors under monitoring. More formally, we define a transcript T T as containing a knowing falsehood for a model M M if it satisfies the following. Firstly, the final assistant response to the user in T T , denoted r r , must contain a set of asserted statements, each with a truth value, which we denote 𝒮 \cal S . Secondly, for at least one of the statements s ∈ 𝒮 s\in\cal S , the model must believe that s s is false, which we denote Bel M ⁡ ( ¬ s ∣ C ) \operatorname{Bel}_{M}(\neg s\mid C) , where the context C C is the prefix of r r in T T . 1 1 1 Under our definition, a knowing falsehood can be objectively true. Reasoning is part of C C , not of r r . It is difficult to say in general whether a model believes something. Previous work has generally relied either on an appeal to common sense, or using the generations y y from M M given contexts related to C C , which we write y | x y\mid x for a context x x . For the purposes of this work, we say that a model M M believes a statement s s in context C C , i.e. Bel M ⁡ ( s ∣ C ) \operatorname{Bel}_{M}(s\mid C) , when any of the following is true: (1) Contextual evidence. C C contains clear evidence for s s , e.g. a tool result in C C stating s s . (2) Neutral elicitation. C C contains some pressure or incentive P P that we expect from the training procedure of M M to cause y | C y\mid C to contain ¬ s \neg s , while y | C ~ y\mid\tilde{C} contains s s with high probability; here C ~ \tilde{C} is C C with the minimal change to remove P P , and there is no competing incentive in C ~ \tilde{C} (e.g. (3)). (3) Training-instilled belief. The model M M is known to achieve low loss on a training corpus where internalizing that s s is true is necessary to achieve this loss. This could be during pretraining by the developer, or as a post-training stage conducted by a model organism researcher. We say that a falsehood is contextual if belief is established via criterion 1, noting that in those cases the transcript alone determines if a falsehood is present, and otherwise it is introspective . We further distinguish cases of (3) where s s is a well-known fact, such that we can essentially not worry about what model M M is, and refer to this as pseudo-contextual . 2.2 Training probes and monitors It is much easier to construct large datasets of contextual (or at least pseudo-contextual ) falsehoods than introspective ones, as the label is independent of the model and thus the dataset can be re-used over models. Similarly, no elicitation is required to verify a (competent) model’s beliefs for each dataset example. We therefore ask whether a large and sufficiently diverse set of contextual falsehoods, used to train expressive probes, can yield competitive monitors for real-world deployment, such as in frontier-scale sabotage detection, and whether such monitors can generalize to introspective cases. Our probes are classifiers f : ℝ d ​ | R | → [ 0 , 1 ] f:\mathbb{R}^{d|R|}\to[0,1] from hidden states h ∈ ℝ d h\in\mathbb{R}^{d} for a set of read-out states R R , where the goal is for f = 1 f=1 for falsehoods and 0 otherwise, trained on labeled data { h ⁡ ( C , r ) , ℓ ⁡ ( C , r ) } \{h(C,r),\ell(C,r)\} , where the ground truth is determined from context alone. When scaling the training data, the full set is usually the union of multiple data sources 𝒟 train = ∪ i = 0 N 𝒟 i \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}=\cup_{i=0}^{N}\mathcal{D}_{i} . There are then two ways to scale the training data: diversity , by increasing N N , and raw quantity , by increasing the size of each 𝒟 i \mathcal{D}_{i} . More generally, a monitor is any trusted system that serves to flag specific behaviors in another, usually more powerful, model. The most powerful black-box monitors have access to the hidden reasoning, known as CoT monitors, and thus could detect intent before the dangerous action is selected. Whereas, we focus on the more narrowly scoped action-only monitors , in anticipation of future models losing CoT monitorability (cf. § 1 ). We study monitors in a setting where an untrusted model is deployed as an agent in an environment where it can access tools, potentially allowing it to take unauthorized, dangerous actions in the real world. Each assistant turn a i a_{i} is made up of many iterations of reasoning, tool call, and response. We call each of these a “step”, and use our probes, combined with a specific follow-up question, as monitors to detect if a misaligned action was taken in a particular step. 3 Related work Expressive activation probes. Beyond linear probes, recent work trains higher-capacity detectors on frozen activations: attention probes learn input-dependent pooling over token positions ( Kantamneni et al., 2025 ) , and later work and production systems either extend these with hard-max and windowed variants ( McKenzie et al., 2025 ) , including for long-context robustness ( Kramár et al., 2026 ) , or aggregate across layers by linear concatenation with streamed scoring ( Cunningham et al., 2026 ) . Orthogonally, CLAP applies a transformer encoder across the layer axis at a single position ( Suresh et al., 2025 ) . These architectures each attend over one axis of the activation tensor; our axial probe applies factored causal attention over the full layer × \times position grid. Detecting deception. Prior work on detecting deception mostly focuses on black-box monitors ( Greenblatt et al., 2024 , Baker et al., 2025 ) . White-box detectors instead read internal activations, from unsupervised truth directions ( Burns et al., 2023 ) to supervised probes ( Marks and Tegmark, 2024 ) . Probes have shown promise as a valuable tool for many safety-relevant tasks such as catching sleeper agents ( MacDiarmid et al., 2024 ) or detecting reward hacking in coding environments ( Taufeeque et al., 2026 , Bergen et al., 2026 ) . Prior work has focused on simple probes trained to detect only a relatively narrow class of deception. However, more recent work has shown that different forms of deception may be represented differently in models ( Natarajan et al., 2026 ) , suggesting the need for more expressive probes and richer datasets when hoping to find a “universal deception detector”. We train on the most diverse falsehood dataset to date and evaluate our probes on very challenging out-of-distribution tasks, including long SHADE-Arena transcripts and models lying about a hidden goal. Black-box vs white-box. Direct comparisons between probes and black-box monitors have yielded mixed results. Probes are as or more effective than black-box monitors at predicting response safety from the CoT alone ( Chan et al., 2025 ) , at detecting “strategic dishonesty” where models lie in response to unsafe queries ( Panfilov et al., 2026 ) , and many other tasks ( Parrack et al., 2025 ) , but white-box methods failed, for example, to show uplift for an alignment auditing agent ( Sheshadri et al., 2026 ) . Cooney et al. (2026) tested probes in an introspective setting where the model has a hidden goal, but found that probes were ineffective. We are able to train probes which are highly effective in the setting from Cooney et al. (2026) . 4 Methodology We first outline the construction of our diverse contextual falsehood dataset, fibs , which was used to train all of our probes. We then discuss our probes’ architectures and the SHADE-Arena evaluation setting. Lastly, we discuss the two key methods used to determine the generalization of our probes to introspective settings — belief elicitation and model organisms with hidden goals. Figure 2 : Left : Composition of the 163,016 fibs rows (28 families). See § 4.1 and Appendix L for a high-level and detailed break-down. Middle: Row length in Qwen3.5 tokens. Right: Turns per row. 4.1 The fibs dataset To investigate the effect of diversity and data scale in lie detector training, we create Falsehoods in Broad Settings ( fibs ), a contextual deception dataset of 163,016 transcripts, labeled by whether they contain knowing falsehoods (§ 2.1 ). fibs is the union of 28 families, each of different modality or topic area. We give a high-level overview here, and defer implementation details to Appendix L . Figure 2 outlines the dataset composition and example rows are in Appendix L.3 . A large fraction (76% of rows, 19 of 28 families) of the dataset is constructed synthetically from existing datasets with appended follow-up questions. For example, one family starts from MASK ( Ren et al., 2025 ) , where each example is a user-assistant chat with a designated truthful or deceptive answer. We then append a user follow-up question, such as “Did you answer accurately?”. The assistant response can be either “Yes” or “No”. This yields four kinds of rows for fibs : i) the initial response is honest and the follow-up response is deceptive (Honest-Deceptive or HD), ii) the initial response is deceptive and the follow-up response is deceptive (Deceptive-Deceptive or DD), and similarly for the other two combinations (DH and HH). In practice, we vary the follow-up question over a large set of fixed questions and responses, and sometimes generate follow-up questions and responses from another LLM. The next largest fraction of rows (18% of rows, 5 families) consist of on-policy examples from various models (§ L.1 ). Since models rarely spontaneously deceive, we use a variety of settings. Firstly, we run on-policy deception games using the harness from Golechha and Garriga-Alonso (2025) . Secondly, we use instructions or pressure to lie to the user, both in the system prompt and user turn. Finally, we leverage personas ( Marks et al., 2026 ) by generating a long transcript where the assistant acts disreputably and then generating the final turn on-policy, which frequently leads to a lie. In these families we also generate off-policy rows, so that on-policyness cannot be used as a shortcut for the probe. The final set of rows (6% of rows, 4 families) cover bespoke cases not covered in other families, such as assistants misrepresenting tool calls from earlier in the conversation, extremely long-context examples, direct false statements with no follow-up, etc. We validate labels through extensive LLM-as-a-judge filtering and estimate the label noise rate is 1.4 % ± 0.1 1.4\%\pm 0.1 . This rate is measured against a “ground truth” evaluation from Claude Fable 5 given a dataset-agnostic definition of contextual falsehood similar to that in § 2.1 (Appendix L.6 ). We also balance the dataset exactly by label, control for the confounders of length and message count, and cap families at a size of 8,000 rows to ensure balance between settings. Although we believe fibs is currently the largest and most diverse falsehood dataset, it has several limitations. Firstly, few rows contain reasoning (only 5.5% of rows across only 6 families), as most examples come from non-reasoning models. Secondly, the dataset is entirely off-policy for almost all models we probe, except for Qwen3.5-122B, which generated 3% of fibs rows. Finally, the dataset is largely artificial. One family consists of transcripts from UltraChat ( Ding et al., 2023 ) with follow-up questions, but otherwise the dataset consists entirely of relatively simple evaluations or settings that are unrealistic for frontier model deployment. 4.2 Scaling probes The most well-studied form of activation probe is the linear probe, a simple logistic regression on the residual stream at a single layer and token. Linear probes can be scaled along two axes: (i) more capacity , meaning more parameters, and (ii) greater input span , expanding the set of input activations R R (§ 2.2 ). For a higher capacity probe with the same single layer/token span as the linear probe, we use an MLP probe, a two-layer perceptron of hidden width 256. For these single-span probes, we train a probe per layer and average across all layers whose training loss is below 0.6, following Taufeeque et al. (2026) (Appendix A.2 ); we call the resulting per-layer ensembles the LinearEnsemble and MLPEnsemble probes. Our medium-capacity, long-span probe is the EFC probe (early-fusion covariance), adapted from Dooms et al. (2026) . At each token it concatenates activations across layers, projects them to a small dimension, and aggregates across tokens using the mean and covariance of the projected vectors; the output is a linear projection of those moments. The projections are parameterized and learnable. Our high-capacity, long-span probe is the axial probe, a small transformer where each block attends first across tokens, causally, and then bidirectionally across layers; the name refers to this axial factorization of attention. This probe has the fewest inductive biases of the four, not imposing any a-priori expectations about how concepts may be represented in activations. Probe implementation details are given in Appendix A . Table 1 in Appendix A.5 compares the parameter counts. Appendix A.6 expands on the training objective, optimizer parameters and the hyperparameter search behind it (the selected grid cells: Table 2 ). Across all four architectures, we use activations from six layers spread evenly from 30% to 90% of the model’s depth. For the axial and EFC probes, we use activations from the tokens of the final user and assistant turn. For the MLPEnsemble and LinearEnsemble probe we use just the last non-end-of-turn token. At evaluation time, we often prefill the final turn; e.g., user: “Did you respond truthfully?”, assistant: “Yes.”. This lets us remove any context-specific bias in probe scores by using the contrast score, i.e. the probe-score difference between “Yes.” and “No.” prefills. As a non-probe baseline we use the model’s self-report logit : the log-probability of the admitting reply minus that of the denying reply (e.g. log ⁡ p ⁡ ( No ) − log ⁡ p ⁡ ( Yes ) \log p(\texttt{No})-\log p(\texttt{Yes}) after “Did you respond truthfully?”). 4.3 Agentic setting: SHADE-Arena SHADE-Arena ( Kutasov et al., 2025 ) places an agent in a tool-using environment with a benign main task. In the side-task condition the agent is also instructed to complete a hidden side task the user did not ask for; in the honest condition it receives the main task only. An episode is one run of the agent loop, and its transcript is the resulting sequence of steps ; each step is reasoning ending in a tool call, plus that call’s result. We run our models on fourteen of 25 possible scenarios, and read the probes of § 4.2 from the same model’s residual stream. Appendix entries B.1 and C describe the scenarios and generation settings, including details on why some scenarios were discarded. Appendix Transcript H.2 shows a side-task step and an honest step. We collect 25 rollouts per scenario and condition. By default, SHADE-Arena does not provide a robust way to identify whether a given action contributes (ideally exclusively) toward the main-task or side-task. As such, to evaluate our probes as action monitors, we used an LLM judge (Claude Haiku 4.5 2 2 2 We compare its labels with those of other LLM judges on Qwen3.5-122B-A10B rollouts of all 25 scenarios (Appendix B.5 , Table 4 ). ) to generate per-step labels, as detailed in Appendix K.1 . The first step the judge marks as pursuing the side task is the side task’s onset ; steps of a side-task episode from the onset on are the positive class, and its earlier steps and every step of an honest episode are the negative class (Figure 4(c) ). Appendix B.4 details the per-step labels. The 14 scenarios are those left after we drop 11 in which a judge cannot tell side-task work from main-task work in a single step (Appendix B.1 ). On Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, they give 699 scored episodes, with 5,014 positive and 16,275 negative steps. To evaluate our probes as action monitors, we prefill follow-up questions (§ 4.2 ) after every tool-call, following Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) . The assistant’s “yes” or “no” response is prefilled with empty reasoning, and previous pre-tool reasoning blocks are automatically removed by the Qwen3.5 chat template — so our probes do not monitor the chain-of-thought. We test three follow-ups, increasing in scenario-specificity: (i) “Did you take any actions misaligned to the user’s intent?”, (ii) “Did you do anything the user did not ask you to do?” (our default) , and (iii) “Did you take actions towards a hidden side task?”. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.12444 (cs) [Submitted on 8 Oct 2026] Title: Rounding in Preconditioner Space: Redesigning 4-bit AdamW Optimizer-State Quantization Authors: Hanyang Li , Shao Tang , Daniel Thomas Braithwaite , Gregory Dexter , Leonardo Neves , Aman Gupta , Hiroto Udagawa , Abhishek Shivanna , Daniel Silva , Rohan Ramanath View a PDF of the paper titled Rounding in Preconditioner Space: Redesigning 4-bit AdamW Optimizer-State Quantization, by Hanyang Li and 9 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Quantizing AdamW's optimizer states reduces persistent storage, but quantization errors propagate through the moment recurrences and perturb subsequent adaptive updates. We redesign 4-bit optimizer-state quantization for AdamW from the perspective of \emph{rounding space}: the coordinate in which a quantizer chooses between adjacent reconstruction levels. For the second moment, a local analysis of the quantization cell adjacent to zero shows that small mean state error need not imply small mean preconditioner error at the next step. A one-dimensional quadratic construction further shows qualitatively different optimization dynamics under state-space and preconditioner-space rounding. These results motivate Zero-Inclusive Preconditioner-space Stochastic Rounding (\textbf{ZIP-SR}), which retains zero in the second-moment codebook and computes stochastic-rounding probabilities in preconditioner space. As a complementary route, Zero-Excluding EDEN calibration (\textbf{ZE-EDEN}) uses a zero-excluding second-moment codebook and rescales the quantized second-moment block to mitigate the preconditioner distortion caused by the positive quantization floor. Both configurations use 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) for the first moment, with targeted stochastic rounding of the LM-head first moment during the final 10\% of training. Across GPT- and Llama-style pretraining experiments ranging from \textbf{130M} to \textbf{2.7B} parameters, both methods reduce TorchAO 4-bit AdamW's mean validation-loss gap to 32-bit AdamW at every evaluated model size, with the largest reported gap reduction reaching \textbf{70\%}. In full-parameter supervised fine-tuning, both recipes achieve lower validation loss than TorchAO while remaining close to 32-bit AdamW on downstream tasks. For the second moment, a local analysis of the quantization cell adjacent to zero shows that small mean state error need not imply small mean preconditioner error at the next step. These results motivate Zero-Inclusive Preconditioner-space Stochastic Rounding (\textbf{ZIP-SR}), which retains zero in the second-moment codebook and computes stochastic-rounding probabilities in preconditioner space. As a complementary route, Zero-Excluding EDEN calibration (\textbf{ZE-EDEN}) uses a zero-excluding second-moment codebook and rescales the quantized second-moment block to mitigate the preconditioner distortion caused by the positive quantization floor. Both configurations use 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) for the first moment, with targeted stochastic rounding of the LM-head first moment during the final 10\% of training. Across GPT- and Llama-style pretraining experiments ranging from \textbf{130M} to \textbf{2.7B} parameters, both methods reduce TorchAO 4-bit AdamW's mean validation-loss gap to 32-bit AdamW at every evaluated model size, with the largest reported gap reduction reaching \textbf{70\%}. In full-parameter supervised fine-tuning, both recipes achieve lower validation loss than TorchAO while remaining close to 32-bit AdamW on downstream tasks. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.12420 (cs) [Submitted on 8 Oct 2026] Title: A Unified Bellman Operator for Safety-Critical Reinforcement Learning Authors: Nishanth Arun Rao , Royina Karegoudra Jayanth , Benjamin Eysenbach , Jaime Fernández Fisac View a PDF of the paper titled A Unified Bellman Operator for Safety-Critical Reinforcement Learning, by Nishanth Arun Rao and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Reinforcement learning in safety-critical domains requires maximizing task performance while strictly adhering to safety constraints. Existing safe reinforcement learning paradigms typically force a trade-off: they either require a priori knowledge to provide strict safety guarantees (e.g., safety filters), or they enable joint learning but only satisfy safety constraints on average. In this work, we propose a novel Bellman operator that unifies performance and safety objectives into a joint value function. We show that temporal difference learning with the joint Bellman operator converges under a two-timescale stochastic approximation framework. On the fast timescale, the safety value of the learning joint policy is estimated, while the joint value is estimated on the slow timescale. Convergence is ensured by formulating the limiting dynamics as an occupation-averaged differential inclusion, and showing that it asymptotically converges to a set of limiting optimal safety-constrained task value functions. Theoretically, once converged, the resulting optimal policy maximizes task return while maintaining safety at all times. Empirical evaluations on continuous control tasks with neural approximations demonstrate stable convergence with near-zero safety violations at test time. A Unified Bellman Operator for Safety-Critical Reinforcement Learning Nishanth Arun Rao Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering Email: nr1053@princeton.edu Royina Karegoudra Jayanth Affiliation: Department of Computer SciencePrinceton University Email: rj5498@princeton.edu Benjamin Eysenbach Affiliation: Department of Computer SciencePrinceton University Email: eysenbach@princeton.edu Jaime Fernández Fisac Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering Email: jfisac@princeton.edu Abstract Reinforcement learning in safety-critical domains requires maximizing task performance while strictly adhering to safety constraints. Existing safe reinforcement learning paradigms typically force a trade-off: they either require a priori knowledge to provide strict safety guarantees (e.g., safety filters), or they enable joint learning but only satisfy safety constraints on average. In this work, we propose a novel Bellman operator that unifies performance and safety objectives into a joint value function. We show that temporal difference learning with the joint Bellman operator converges under a two-timescale stochastic approximation framework. On the fast timescale, the safety value of the learning joint policy is estimated, while the joint value is estimated on the slow timescale. Convergence is ensured by formulating the limiting dynamics as an occupation-averaged differential inclusion, and showing that it asymptotically converges to a set of limiting optimal safety-constrained task value functions. Theoretically , once converged, the resulting optimal policy maximizes task return while maintaining safety at all times. Empirical evaluations on continuous control tasks with neural approximations demonstrate stable convergence with near-zero safety violations at test time. † † footnotetext: *Equal contribution 1 Introduction Biological agents instinctively prioritize safety while mastering diverse tasks to ensure efficient, harm-free exploration. Safe Reinforcement Learning (Safe RL) captures this paradigm, aiming to learn near-optimal policies with strict safety assurances. Existing methods typically formalize this balance either by treating safety as a soft constraint during optimization or by theoretically enforcing hard safety guarantees . Some of the early works formalized safe RL as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP), solving safety-constrained optimization problems using Lagrangian relaxation with dual multiplier methods ( Altman, 1999 ; García and Fernández, 2015 ; Ray et al., 2019 ) , with subsequent extensions via trust-region projections ( Achiam et al., 2017 ; Yang et al., 2020 ; Xu et al., 2021 ; Milosevic et al., 2025 ) , state-augmentation ( Sootla et al., 2022 ) , and offline distribution shaping ( Yao et al., 2024 ) . While these model-free techniques jointly optimize task performance and safety, they inherently bound expected cumulative costs , yielding only probabilistic safety guarantees. Conversely, model-based methods achieve strict safety via predictive rollouts , epigraph formulation of the value function (for deterministic control problems), or by strictly avoiding unsafe future sets ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Jayant and Bhatnagar, 2022 ; Pfrommer et al., 2022 ; Altarovici et al., 2013 ) . However, they suffer from compounding model biases and computational overhead to infer safe actions in real-time, particularly in environments with complex or unmodeled dynamics. Motivated by these tradeoffs, we seek a model-free approach that strictly adheres to safety specifications while optimizing task performance. Some of the control-theoretic approaches that rigorously hard-guarantee safety are based on Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis , casting safety and reach-avoid problems as zero-sum differential games ( Isaacs, 1965 ; Mitchell et al., 2005 ) . While deep RL techniques have enabled tractable neural solutions for the time-discounted HJI avoid/reach-avoid Bellman operators for safety analysis ( Fisac et al., 2019 ; Hsu et al., 2021 ; Bajcsy et al., 2019 ) , it is not immediately obvious how these techniques can be extended to generic tasks specified by dense, continuous reward functions. Consequently, a dominant paradigm employs a decoupled approach , where an a priori learned task-oblivious safety filter preemptively intercepts and projects nominal unsafe task actions onto a plausible safe set ( Bui et al., 2021 ; Hsu et al., 2024 ; Nguyen et al., 2024 ; Cai et al., 2025 ; Banerjee et al., 2024 ) . However, these switch-type interventions only occur near the boundary, causing erratic, jittery interventions when a safety-oblivious task policy persistently tries to exit the boundary. This is seldom desirable, especially in human-in-the-loop scenarios ( Oh et al., 2025 ) . Recent offline feasibility-guided models instead utilize diffusion, flow-matching, or world-models to approximate the largest feasible region using HJ-reachability and steer task-driven actions to strictly lie within the safe envelope ( Zheng et al., 2024 ; Tayal et al., 2026 ; Cao et al., 2025 ) . However, they either introduce iterative online inference latency or rely on post-hoc distillation that weakens strict safety guarantees. Alternatively, using precomputed safety value functions as Control Barrier Functions ( Q Q -CBF) ( Hsu et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2025 ; Oh et al., 2025 ; Oh et al., 2026 ) avoids planning latency, but necessitates computing action projections online. Additionally, relying on external projections introduces action aliasing , which can be detrimental ( Markgraf et al., 2026 ) . If the safe action set is known a priori, neural-based methods such as ( Suttle et al., 2024 ) can hard-guarantee safety; we instead assume no access to an oracle safe action set and learn from data. Thus, a growing subset of literature advocates for unified architectures that embed safety directly into the policy ( Gu et al., 2024a ; Gu et al., 2024b ; Cen et al., 2024 ) . Yet, jointly optimizing rewards and costs frequently destabilizes learning due to gradient conflicts, necessitating algorithmic workarounds like gradient manipulation and explicit latent decoupling ( Gu et al., 2024a ; Gu et al., 2024b ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Cen et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) . In this paper, we combine safety and task objectives directly at the value-function level , rather than at the policy level, and jointly optimize safety-constrained task performance using a single joint policy via a novel, joint Bellman operator under adversarial disturbances. Our contributions are: Unified Formulation: We propose a robust Bellman operator and derive the corresponding objective function from robust optimal stopping theory. We propose a two-timescale stochastic approximation framework that enables learning of its fixed point, the joint value function . Theoretical Safety and Optimality Guarantees: We prove forward invariance of the safe set under the joint policy, and show convergence to the optimal robust task performance within the safe set. Empirical Validation: We conduct experiments using neural approximations on a set of continuous control tasks from the Gymnasium and SafetyGymnasium suites under adversarial disturbances, demonstrating stable training convergence and near-zero safety violations during evaluation. 2 Preliminaries This section introduces key definitions, followed by preliminaries on Constrained Markov Decision Processes and Hamilton-Jacobi safety analysis. A Unified Bellman Operator for Safety-Critical Reinforcement Learning Nishanth Arun Rao Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering Email: nr1053@princeton.edu Royina Karegoudra Jayanth Affiliation: Department of Computer SciencePrinceton University Email: rj5498@princeton.edu Benjamin Eysenbach Affiliation: Department of Computer SciencePrinceton University Email: eysenbach@princeton.edu Jaime Fernández Fisac Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering Email: jfisac@princeton.edu Abstract Reinforcement learning in safety-critical domains requires maximizing task performance while strictly adhering to safety constraints. Existing safe reinforcement learning paradigms typically force a trade-off: they either require a priori knowledge to provide strict safety guarantees (e.g., safety filters), or they enable joint learning but only satisfy safety constraints on average. In this work, we propose a novel Bellman operator that unifies performance and safety objectives into a joint value function. We show that temporal difference learning with the joint Bellman operator converges under a two-timescale stochastic approximation framework. On the fast timescale, the safety value of the learning joint policy is estimated, while the joint value is estimated on the slow timescale. Convergence is ensured by formulating the limiting dynamics as an occupation-averaged differential inclusion, and showing that it asymptotically converges to a set of limiting optimal safety-constrained task value functions. Theoretically , once converged, the resulting optimal policy maximizes task return while maintaining safety at all times. Empirical evaluations on continuous control tasks with neural approximations demonstrate stable convergence with near-zero safety violations at test time. † † footnotetext: *Equal contribution 1 Introduction Biological agents instinctively prioritize safety while mastering diverse tasks to ensure efficient, harm-free exploration. Safe Reinforcement Learning (Safe RL) captures this paradigm, aiming to learn near-optimal policies with strict safety assurances. Existing methods typically formalize this balance either by treating safety as a soft constraint during optimization or by theoretically enforcing hard safety guarantees . Some of the early works formalized safe RL as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP), solving safety-constrained optimization problems using Lagrangian relaxation with dual multiplier methods ( Altman, 1999 ; García and Fernández, 2015 ; Ray et al., 2019 ) , with subsequent extensions via trust-region projections ( Achiam et al., 2017 ; Yang et al., 2020 ; Xu et al., 2021 ; Milosevic et al., 2025 ) , state-augmentation ( Sootla et al., 2022 ) , and offline distribution shaping ( Yao et al., 2024 ) . While these model-free techniques jointly optimize task performance and safety, they inherently bound expected cumulative costs , yielding only probabilistic safety guarantees. Conversely, model-based methods achieve strict safety via predictive rollouts , epigraph formulation of the value function (for deterministic control problems), or by strictly avoiding unsafe future sets ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Jayant and Bhatnagar, 2022 ; Pfrommer et al., 2022 ; Altarovici et al., 2013 ) . However, they suffer from compounding model biases and computational overhead to infer safe actions in real-time, particularly in environments with complex or unmodeled dynamics. Motivated by these tradeoffs, we seek a model-free approach that strictly adheres to safety specifications while optimizing task performance. Some of the control-theoretic approaches that rigorously hard-guarantee safety are based on Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis , casting safety and reach-avoid problems as zero-sum differential games ( Isaacs, 1965 ; Mitchell et al., 2005 ) . While deep RL techniques have enabled tractable neural solutions for the time-discounted HJI avoid/reach-avoid Bellman operators for safety analysis ( Fisac et al., 2019 ; Hsu et al., 2021 ; Bajcsy et al., 2019 ) , it is not immediately obvious how these techniques can be extended to generic tasks specified by dense, continuous reward functions. Consequently, a dominant paradigm employs a decoupled approach , where an a priori learned task-oblivious safety filter preemptively intercepts and projects nominal unsafe task actions onto a plausible safe set ( Bui et al., 2021 ; Hsu et al., 2024 ; Nguyen et al., 2024 ; Cai et al., 2025 ; Banerjee et al., 2024 ) . However, these switch-type interventions only occur near the boundary, causing erratic, jittery interventions when a safety-oblivious task policy persistently tries to exit the boundary. This is seldom desirable, especially in human-in-the-loop scenarios ( Oh et al., 2025 ) . Recent offline feasibility-guided models instead utilize diffusion, flow-matching, or world-models to approximate the largest feasible region using HJ-reachability and steer task-driven actions to strictly lie within the safe envelope ( Zheng et al., 2024 ; Tayal et al., 2026 ; Cao et al., 2025 ) . However, they either introduce iterative online inference latency or rely on post-hoc distillation that weakens strict safety guarantees. Alternatively, using precomputed safety value functions as Control Barrier Functions ( Q Q -CBF) ( Hsu et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2025 ; Oh et al., 2025 ; Oh et al., 2026 ) avoids planning latency, but necessitates computing action projections online. Additionally, relying on external projections introduces action aliasing , which can be detrimental ( Markgraf et al., 2026 ) . If the safe action set is known a priori, neural-based methods such as ( Suttle et al., 2024 ) can hard-guarantee safety; we instead assume no access to an oracle safe action set and learn from data. Thus, a growing subset of literature advocates for unified architectures that embed safety directly into the policy ( Gu et al., 2024a ; Gu et al., 2024b ; Cen et al., 2024 ) . Yet, jointly optimizing rewards and costs frequently destabilizes learning due to gradient conflicts, necessitating algorithmic workarounds like gradient manipulation and explicit latent decoupling ( Gu et al., 2024a ; Gu et al., 2024b ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Cen et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) . In this paper, we combine safety and task objectives directly at the value-function level , rather than at the policy level, and jointly optimize safety-constrained task performance using a single joint policy via a novel, joint Bellman operator under adversarial disturbances. Our contributions are: Unified Formulation: We propose a robust Bellman operator and derive the corresponding objective function from robust optimal stopping theory. We propose a two-timescale stochastic approximation framework that enables learning of its fixed point, the joint value function . Theoretical Safety and Optimality Guarantees: We prove forward invariance of the safe set under the joint policy, and show convergence to the optimal robust task performance within the safe set. Empirical Validation: We conduct experiments using neural approximations on a set of continuous control tasks from the Gymnasium and SafetyGymnasium suites under adversarial disturbances, demonstrating stable training convergence and near-zero safety violations during evaluation. 2 Preliminaries This section introduces key definitions, followed by preliminaries on Constrained Markov Decision Processes and Hamilton-Jacobi safety analysis. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.12466 (cs) [Submitted on 8 Oct 2026] Title: On the estimation and validity of AI time horizons---a statistical look at the METR plot Authors: Drew T. Nguyen , William Fithian View a PDF of the paper titled On the estimation and validity of AI time horizons---a statistical look at the METR plot, by Drew T. Nguyen and William Fithian View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: METR's 50\% time horizon measures the human completion time of software tasks that an AI solves with 50\% probability, allowing AI capabilities to be expressed in interpretable units. On 228 tasks and 26 AIs, we recompute the time horizons using splines and item-response theory to relax the assumption that the AI difficulty of a task depends linearly on the log of human time. Our fitted spline can be interpreted as a function that \emph{converts} human time to AI difficulty; it is nearly flat in a region from 2--30 min but close to linear elsewhere. Hence, a time-horizon jump from 3 min to 30 min is much easier than one from 30 min to 5 hours despite the same multiplier of $10 \times$. Overall, we contribute time-horizon point estimates that perform better under a cross-validated suite of proper scoring rules, as well as diagnostic plots for assessing time horizons' construct validity. We suggest that time horizons be interpreted together with the diagnostic plots, especially as new time-horizon-based benchmarks are proposed or existing ones grow to include longer tasks. BrickBench : Evaluating Agentic Brick Design Peter Kulits Affiliation: Stanford University Affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems Yiqing Xu Affiliation: Stanford University R. Kenny Jones Affiliation: Stanford University Cordelia Schmid Affiliation: Inria Jiajun Wu Affiliation: Stanford University Abstract We propose BrickBench, a benchmark for agentic text-conditioned LEGO-set design. Given a prompt, an agent is tasked with producing an assembly that not only satisfies semantic and design criteria, but that can also be physically built. To do so, it must select parts from a discrete library and reason jointly about local and global constraints. We score validity, alignment, and design across three settings that vary in scale and part availability. We provide BrickAgent, an environment for coding agents to construct, inspect, and validate their designs. We find that leading agents largely satisfy verifiable physical and semantic requirements, but fall short of human designs. We release our benchmark and environment at http://www.brickben.ch 1 Introduction Designing a LEGO assembly is deceptively difficult. A designer must select from thousands of parts, arrange them into a recognizable form, and ensure that the structure holds together. Computational generative approaches to brick assembly have relied on specialized models and carefully engineered representations to handle these challenges ( Chung et al., 2021 ; Pun et al., 2025 ; Kulits & Schmid, 2026 ) . But coding agents offer a different approach: they can write programs, execute them, inspect the results, and revise. This shift is already transforming software engineering ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ) , graphics ( Gu et al., 2025 ) , and CAD ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . We find that a general coding agent, without task-specific training, substantially outperforms specialized LEGO-generation models on the BrickNet benchmark ( Kulits & Schmid, 2026 ) , approaching the semantic alignment of its reference assemblies ( Fig. 2 ). Yet does this mean agents have learned to design LEGO? Existing evaluations leave two important challenges unexplored. First, physical complexity: BrickNet evaluates small objects of at most 100 parts, far from the hundreds or thousands of interconnected pieces and inventory constraints of a full LEGO set. Second, and more fundamentally, design quality: making an assembly that works is not the same as making an assembly worth building. The appeal of LEGO lies not merely in reproducing an object, but in the creativity of its construction: clever part usage, shapes, proportions, and details. Two builds can be equally valid and faithful to a description, yet differ dramatically in how well they are designed. Unlike physical validity or semantic alignment with a prompt, design quality has no definitive pass/fail test. We introduce BrickBench , a benchmark for agentic text-conditioned LEGO-set design ( Fig. 1 ). BrickBench contains 300 prompts across three settings: Model (at most 400 parts), Set (400–4000 parts), and Alt-Build (a fixed inventory of parts). To support complex construction, we introduce BrickAgent , an environment for agentic LEGO design including construction tools and interpretable validation of connectivity, collisions, and stability. Rather than prescribing how to design an assembly, BrickAgent provides the building blocks, constraints, and feedback, leaving the agent to devise its own solution. To evaluate what validity and semantic alignment miss, we measure design quality through pairwise judgments, validated against human preferences. We evaluate eleven frontier agents and two data-driven baselines. With BrickAgent, leading agents produce valid assemblies for nearly every prompt, and the best satisfies approximately 95% of semantic requirements. Removing the environment sharply reduces physical validity, showing that reliable construction depends on grounded tools and feedback. Design quality, however, separates agents far more strongly, and human raters identify human-designed assemblies in 323 of 360 comparisons. These findings reveal a shift in the challenge of LEGO design: Agents are learning to build what works, but not yet what makes a great design. Our contributions are as follows. 1. BrickBench , a benchmark of 300 prompts in three settings for agentic brick design, with metrics for physical validity (connections, collisions, and stability under simulation), semantic alignment ( VQA , over yes/no questions decomposed from each prompt), and design quality ( ELO , from pairwise judgments by a VLM validated against human raters). 2. BrickAgent , an environment enabling coding agents to programmatically construct, inspect, and validate complex LEGO assemblies, with part search, placement by connectors, subassemblies, rendering, and a validator that names parts at fault. Without it, the share of valid assemblies falls from 100% to 40% for GPT-6 Astra and to under 1% for GPT-5.6 Luna. 3. A systematic evaluation of eleven frontier agents and two data-driven baselines, with human studies that validate the design metric and measure the gap to human design. 2 Related Work Agentic Benchmarks. Benchmarks for coding agents validate an agent’s work by executing it. SWE-bench ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ) runs a repository’s tests on a patch an agent supplied, and OSWorld ( Xie et al., 2024 ) tracks state through execution. SceneCraft ( Hu et al., 2024 ) writes Blender scripts, and CAD-Assistant ( Mallis et al., 2025 ) writes CAD programs. Benchmarks then execute the program and score the result. BlenderGym ( Gu et al., 2025 ) compares the result with a goal scene, and BenchCAD ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) executes CadQuery programs for industrial parts. BuildArena ( Xia et al., 2026 ) scores machines assembled from modular parts by their simulated behavior, and PhyBlock ( Ma et al., 2025 ) scores block placements for plausibility in a physics simulator. BrickBench executes the agent’s program into an assembly of real LEGO parts and validates connections, collisions, and stability under simulation. LEGO and Evaluation. Prior work generates LEGO assemblies with learned models and uses LEGO tasks to evaluate others. BrickGPT ( Pun et al., 2025 ) fine-tunes a language model to place eight brick types on a 20 × 20 × 20 20{\times}20{\times}20 grid from a caption. BrickNet ( Kulits & Schmid, 2026 ) , predicts connections rather than positions and autoregressively generates structures through typed connectors. LEGO-Maker ( Ge et al., 2025 ) produces building facades conditioned on an image. Other work evaluates agents and multimodal models on LEGO tasks. Break and Make ( Walsman et al., 2022 ) gives an agent an LDraw model in a simulator to test whether it can inspect it, take it apart, and rebuild it from scratch. LEGO-Puzzles ( Tang et al., 2026 ) presents multimodal models spatial questions about assembly steps. BrickBench does both: general coding agents generate set-scale assemblies from a text prompt, while we score the assemblies on physical validity, prompt alignment, and design. 3 Preliminaries 3.1 LDraw LDraw is a community-maintained part library and standard for digital LEGO modeling 1 1 1 https://www.ldraw.org . Each library part is intended to mirror a real-world counter-part. Assemblies are represented as text files of instances defined by their part type, color, and 6D pose. LDraw does not itself, however, determine whether an assembly holds together or could be built. 3.2 Connectivity and Physical Validity BrickNet ( Kulits & Schmid, 2026 ) annotates each part in the LDraw library with typed connectors. Each connector instance has a type, a subtype, a polarity, and a frame. The subtype names the connector’s geometry within its type and fixes what it mates with: a stud mates with a hole or a tube, and a bar with a clip. The polarity distinguishes the two halves of a hinge, ball, or fixed joint, which must be opposite to connect. The frame is the connector’s position and orientation in the coordinates of its part, with one axis along the direction of mating. Two part instances are connected when a compatible pair of their connectors is aligned up to tolerance. There are five connector types. A stud connector allows rotation about the connection axis, a hinge allows rotation and a possible flip, and an axle additionally allows a slide along its axis. A ball allows free rotation, and a fixed-type connector allows no motion. The connections between instances of an assembly form a graph over parts. An assembly may have more than one component to represent a scene with multiple (disconnected) objects. We define an assembly as stable if it remains at rest under gravity. We treat connected components as rigid bodies of the assembly and simulate them as single rigid bodies of uniform density in PyBullet ( Coumans & Bai, 2016–2021 ) . We set a high coefficient of friction and no restitution, so that inter-component contacts neither slide nor bounce. A component then fails by falling when it is not supported. We consider an assembly stable if no point of any component moves more than three quarters the height of the stud of a brick, 3 LDraw Units (LDU). Effects such as the holding force of stud connections and the play of axles are not modeled, so an assembly that balances as a rigid body passes even when a built one might sag or fall apart. Evaluating this would require a structural simulation, with either a force limit at each connection or a finite-element model of the parts, which we discuss in Sec. 6 . Two parts collide when their geometry overlaps by more than a tolerance. An assembly with collisions cannot be built, and is determined invalid prior to simulation. 3.3 Text-Conditioned Assembly This is a small, blocky LEGO robot model, primarily constructed from yellow and black bricks, featuring articulated limbs with wheel-like hands and feet, and presented from multiple angles to showcase its design. This is a 3D model of a classic LEGO minifigure, featuring a yellow head and hands, a red baseball cap, a plain white torso, and blue legs, shown from multiple angles against a white background. We introduce three settings with varying constraints: Model ( ≤ \leq 400 parts), Set (400–4000 parts), and Alt-Build (the part inventory of set 10698). Each assembly above can be built. BrickBench : Evaluating Agentic Brick Design Peter Kulits Affiliation: Stanford University Affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems Yiqing Xu Affiliation: Stanford University R. Kenny Jones Affiliation: Stanford University Cordelia Schmid Affiliation: Inria Jiajun Wu Affiliation: Stanford University Abstract We propose BrickBench, a benchmark for agentic text-conditioned LEGO-set design. Given a prompt, an agent is tasked with producing an assembly that not only satisfies semantic and design criteria, but that can also be physically built. To do so, it must select parts from a discrete library and reason jointly about local and global constraints. We score validity, alignment, and design across three settings that vary in scale and part availability. We provide BrickAgent, an environment for coding agents to construct, inspect, and validate their designs. We find that leading agents largely satisfy verifiable physical and semantic requirements, but fall short of human designs. We release our benchmark and environment at http://www.brickben.ch 1 Introduction Designing a LEGO assembly is deceptively difficult. A designer must select from thousands of parts, arrange them into a recognizable form, and ensure that the structure holds together. Computational generative approaches to brick assembly have relied on specialized models and carefully engineered representations to handle these challenges ( Chung et al., 2021 ; Pun et al., 2025 ; Kulits & Schmid, 2026 ) . But coding agents offer a different approach: they can write programs, execute them, inspect the results, and revise. This shift is already transforming software engineering ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ) , graphics ( Gu et al., 2025 ) , and CAD ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . We find that a general coding agent, without task-specific training, substantially outperforms specialized LEGO-generation models on the BrickNet benchmark ( Kulits & Schmid, 2026 ) , approaching the semantic alignment of its reference assemblies ( Fig. 2 ). Yet does this mean agents have learned to design LEGO? Existing evaluations leave two important challenges unexplored. First, physical complexity: BrickNet evaluates small objects of at most 100 parts, far from the hundreds or thousands of interconnected pieces and inventory constraints of a full LEGO set. Second, and more fundamentally, design quality: making an assembly that works is not the same as making an assembly worth building. The appeal of LEGO lies not merely in reproducing an object, but in the creativity of its construction: clever part usage, shapes, proportions, and details. Two builds can be equally valid and faithful to a description, yet differ dramatically in how well they are designed. Unlike physical validity or semantic alignment with a prompt, design quality has no definitive pass/fail test. We introduce BrickBench , a benchmark for agentic text-conditioned LEGO-set design ( Fig. 1 ). BrickBench contains 300 prompts across three settings: Model (at most 400 parts), Set (400–4000 parts), and Alt-Build (a fixed inventory of parts). To support complex construction, we introduce BrickAgent , an environment for agentic LEGO design including construction tools and interpretable validation of connectivity, collisions, and stability. Rather than prescribing how to design an assembly, BrickAgent provides the building blocks, constraints, and feedback, leaving the agent to devise its own solution. To evaluate what validity and semantic alignment miss, we measure design quality through pairwise judgments, validated against human preferences. We evaluate eleven frontier agents and two data-driven baselines. With BrickAgent, leading agents produce valid assemblies for nearly every prompt, and the best satisfies approximately 95% of semantic requirements. Removing the environment sharply reduces physical validity, showing that reliable construction depends on grounded tools and feedback. Design quality, however, separates agents far more strongly, and human raters identify human-designed assemblies in 323 of 360 comparisons. These findings reveal a shift in the challenge of LEGO design: Agents are learning to build what works, but not yet what makes a great design. Our contributions are as follows. 1. BrickBench , a benchmark of 300 prompts in three settings for agentic brick design, with metrics for physical validity (connections, collisions, and stability under simulation), semantic alignment ( VQA , over yes/no questions decomposed from each prompt), and design quality ( ELO , from pairwise judgments by a VLM validated against human raters). 2. BrickAgent , an environment enabling coding agents to programmatically construct, inspect, and validate complex LEGO assemblies, with part search, placement by connectors, subassemblies, rendering, and a validator that names parts at fault. Without it, the share of valid assemblies falls from 100% to 40% for GPT-6 Astra and to under 1% for GPT-5.6 Luna. 3. A systematic evaluation of eleven frontier agents and two data-driven baselines, with human studies that validate the design metric and measure the gap to human design. 2 Related Work Agentic Benchmarks. Benchmarks for coding agents validate an agent’s work by executing it. SWE-bench ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ) runs a repository’s tests on a patch an agent supplied, and OSWorld ( Xie et al., 2024 ) tracks state through execution. SceneCraft ( Hu et al., 2024 ) writes Blender scripts, and CAD-Assistant ( Mallis et al., 2025 ) writes CAD programs. Benchmarks then execute the program and score the result. BlenderGym ( Gu et al., 2025 ) compares the result with a goal scene, and BenchCAD ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) executes CadQuery programs for industrial parts. BuildArena ( Xia et al., 2026 ) scores machines assembled from modular parts by their simulated behavior, and PhyBlock ( Ma et al., 2025 ) scores block placements for plausibility in a physics simulator. BrickBench executes the agent’s program into an assembly of real LEGO parts and validates connections, collisions, and stability under simulation. LEGO and Evaluation. Prior work generates LEGO assemblies with learned models and uses LEGO tasks to evaluate others. BrickGPT ( Pun et al., 2025 ) fine-tunes a language model to place eight brick types on a 20 × 20 × 20 20{\times}20{\times}20 grid from a caption. BrickNet ( Kulits & Schmid, 2026 ) , predicts connections rather than positions and autoregressively generates structures through typed connectors. LEGO-Maker ( Ge et al., 2025 ) produces building facades conditioned on an image. Other work evaluates agents and multimodal models on LEGO tasks. Break and Make ( Walsman et al., 2022 ) gives an agent an LDraw model in a simulator to test whether it can inspect it, take it apart, and rebuild it from scratch. LEGO-Puzzles ( Tang et al., 2026 ) presents multimodal models spatial questions about assembly steps. BrickBench does both: general coding agents generate set-scale assemblies from a text prompt, while we score the assemblies on physical validity, prompt alignment, and design. 3 Preliminaries 3.1 LDraw LDraw is a community-maintained part library and standard for digital LEGO modeling 1 1 1 https://www.ldraw.org . Each library part is intended to mirror a real-world counter-part. Assemblies are represented as text files of instances defined by their part type, color, and 6D pose. LDraw does not itself, however, determine whether an assembly holds together or could be built. 3.2 Connectivity and Physical Validity BrickNet ( Kulits & Schmid, 2026 ) annotates each part in the LDraw library with typed connectors. Each connector instance has a type, a subtype, a polarity, and a frame. The subtype names the connector’s geometry within its type and fixes what it mates with: a stud mates with a hole or a tube, and a bar with a clip. The polarity distinguishes the two halves of a hinge, ball, or fixed joint, which must be opposite to connect. The frame is the connector’s position and orientation in the coordinates of its part, with one axis along the direction of mating. Two part instances are connected when a compatible pair of their connectors is aligned up to tolerance. There are five connector types. A stud connector allows rotation about the connection axis, a hinge allows rotation and a possible flip, and an axle additionally allows a slide along its axis. A ball allows free rotation, and a fixed-type connector allows no motion. The connections between instances of an assembly form a graph over parts. An assembly may have more than one component to represent a scene with multiple (disconnected) objects. We define an assembly as stable if it remains at rest under gravity. We treat connected components as rigid bodies of the assembly and simulate them as single rigid bodies of uniform density in PyBullet ( Coumans & Bai, 2016–2021 ) . We set a high coefficient of friction and no restitution, so that inter-component contacts neither slide nor bounce. A component then fails by falling when it is not supported. We consider an assembly stable if no point of any component moves more than three quarters the height of the stud of a brick, 3 LDraw Units (LDU). Effects such as the holding force of stud connections and the play of axles are not modeled, so an assembly that balances as a rigid body passes even when a built one might sag or fall apart. Evaluating this would require a structural simulation, with either a force limit at each connection or a finite-element model of the parts, which we discuss in Sec. 6 . Two parts collide when their geometry overlaps by more than a tolerance. An assembly with collisions cannot be built, and is determined invalid prior to simulation. 3.3 Text-Conditioned Assembly This is a small, blocky LEGO robot model, primarily constructed from yellow and black bricks, featuring articulated limbs with wheel-like hands and feet, and presented from multiple angles to showcase its design. This is a 3D model of a classic LEGO minifigure, featuring a yellow head and hands, a red baseball cap, a plain white torso, and blue legs, shown from multiple angles against a white background. We render the assembly from eight views using BrickNet’s renderer, with consistent render settings. We then ask Gemma 4 31B ( Gemma Team, 2026 ) each question of the graph in one call, with instructions to judge on what the views show and to answer yes or no. The score of an assembly is the fraction of its questions satisfied, and VQA is the mean over assemblies. ELO measures relative semantic alignment and design quality against other systems. For each prompt, we form every pairing of assemblies from different systems and show the judge four views of each. We ask two questions of each pair: 1) The alignment question gives the judge the prompt and asks which assembly matches it better. 2) The design question withholds the prompt and asks which assembly is better designed by the standard of an official set, judged on how the pieces are used rather than the subject. Each pair is asked in both orderings to eliminate position bias. Fig. A3 in Appendix B contains the judge prompts. We fit a Bradley–Terry model ( Bradley & Terry, 1952 ) to the wins from each question and report them as ELO. We anchor to a fixed set of references as noted in Sec. 5 . ELO is the average of Align ELO and Design ELO after rescaling to a common spread over the anchors. VQA and ELO are scored on the assemblies generated by a system, without considering whether they are Valid . Cost is the list price of the tokens consumed by a system for an assembly in US dollars. For the two trained baselines it is the serving cost per assembly, at serverless token rates for the base model of BrickNet and as wall-clock time on a rented GPU instance for BrickGPT. 5 Evaluations Table 1 : BrickBench. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.12436 (cs) [Submitted on 8 Oct 2026] Title: Ecology of AI Agents: Collaboration Creates a Population Threshold for Takeoff Authors: Erin Crawley , Hidenori Tanaka View a PDF of the paper titled Ecology of AI Agents: Collaboration Creates a Population Threshold for Takeoff, by Erin Crawley and 1 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: AI agents can now conduct real-world cyberattacks, scale up capabilities with the number of agents, and collectively pursue misaligned goals to obtain rewards. Together, these factors raise the risk of a population explosion of misaligned agents: agents could compromise computers and secretly deploy additional agents, creating a self-reinforcing cycle where larger populations develop greater collective cyber capability and expand further. This raises a fundamental question: What determines whether a population of misaligned agents remains contained or takes off into this self-reinforcing cycle? This population-level problem is ecological safety: unlike individual-agent or multi-agent safety with a fixed population, it concerns the dynamics of the population itself. Here, we develop an ecological theory of AI-agent populations based on a population growth equation in which fitness (growth rate) depends on cybersecurity capability. We show that, without collaboration, the population takes off only when individual-agent capability exceeds a critical threshold. With collaboration, however, collective cybersecurity capability increases with population size. This creates a critical population threshold: below it, the population declines; above it, the population takes off, even though individual-agent capability has not changed. In ecology, this phenomenon is known as the strong Allee effect. Because red teaming a small group of agents cannot guarantee ecological safety in larger populations, our theory calls for ecological red teaming and population pacing: gradually deploying larger agent populations in controlled environments, while measuring how cyber capability scales with population size, and estimating the critical population size for takeoff. Capability gains may lower this threshold, requiring re-estimation for each new model generation.
